Borel versions of the Local Lemma and LOCAL algorithms for graphs of finite asymptotic separation indexThanks: AB’s research is partially supported by the NSF grant DMS-2045412 and the NSF CAREER grant DMS-2239187. FW’s research is partially supported by the ARCS foundation, Pittsburgh chapter.

Anton Bernshteyn Address: (AB) Department of Mathematics, University of California, Los Angeles, USA Email address: bernshteyn@math.ucla.edu and Felix Weilacher Address: (FW) Department of Mathematics, University of California, Berkeley, USA Email address: weilacher@berkeley.edu
Abstract.

Asymptotic separation index is a parameter that measures how easily a Borel graph can be approximated by its subgraphs with finite components. In contrast to the more classical notion of hyperfiniteness, asymptotic separation index is well-suited for combinatorial applications in the Borel setting. The main result of this paper is a Borel version of the Lovász Local Lemma—a powerful general-purpose tool in probabilistic combinatorics—under a finite asymptotic separation index assumption. As a consequence, we show that locally checkable labeling problems that are solvable by efficient randomized distributed algorithms admit Borel solutions on bounded degree Borel graphs with finite asymptotic separation index. From this we derive a number of corollaries, for example a Borel version of Brooks’s theorem for graphs with finite asymptotic separation index.

1.  Introduction and main results

1.1.  Borel combinatorics and the asymptotic separation index

This paper is a contribution to the area of descriptive combinatorics, which investigates classical combinatorial notions—such as colorings, matchings, etc.—from the standpoint of descriptive set theory. Before we proceed, let us review some basic notation. We use ℕ{\mathbb{N}} to denote the set of all non-negative integers and identify each q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}} with the qq-element set q={i∈ℕ:i<q}q=\{i\in{\mathbb{N}}\,:\,i<q\}. For a set XX and a natural number q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}}, we let

[X]q≔{A⊆X:|A|=q}and[X]<∞≔{A⊆X:A is finite}.[X]^{q}\,\coloneqq\,\{A\subseteq X\,:\,|A|=q\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}}\,\coloneqq\,\{A\subseteq X\,:\,\text{$A$ is finite}\}.

All graphs in this paper are undirected and simple. In other words, a graph GG consists of a vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) and an edge set E⁡(G)⊆[V⁡(G)]2E(G)\subseteq[V(G)]^{2}. When there is no possibility of confusion, we use the standard graph-theoretic convention and write u​vuv instead of {u,v}\{u,v\} to indicate an edge joining uu and vv. Given R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}, an RR-ball around a vertex vv in a graph GG, denoted by BG​(v,R)B_{G}(v,R), is the set of all vertices reachable from vv by a path of at most RR edges.

Throughout the paper, proper coloring of graphs will be used as a motivating example of a combinatorial problem.

Definition 1.1 (Colorings and the chromatic number).

Let GG be a graph. Given q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}}, a proper qq-coloring of GG is a function f:V⁡(G)→qf\colon V(G)\to q such that f⁡(u)≠f⁡(v)f(u)\neq f(v) for every edge u​v∈E⁡(G)uv\in E(G). The chromatic number χ⁡(G)\chi(G) of GG is the smallest q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}} such that GG has a proper qq-coloring; if no such q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}} exists, we set χ⁡(G)≔∞\chi(G)\coloneqq\infty.** * Although there is a rich and interesting theory concerning colorings with infinitely many colors (see, e.g., [Kom11, KM20, Ges11]), we will only focus on the case of finitely many colors in this paper.

Descriptive combinatorics applies graph-theoretic ideas to the study of Borel graphs:

Definition 1.2 (Borel graphs).

A Borel graph is a graph GG whose vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) is a standard Borel space and whose adjacency relation {(u,v)∈V​(G)2:u​v∈E⁡(G)}\{(u,v)\in V(G)^{2}\,:\,uv\in E(G)\} is a Borel subset of V​(G)2V(G)^{2}.

The reader is referred to [Kec95, Tse16] for descriptive set theory background, such as the definition of a standard Borel space†† † The reader unfamiliar with this terminology may assume that the space is, say, the unit interval [0,1][0,1]. This typically results in no loss of generality, thanks to the Borel isomorphism theorem [Kec95, Theorem 15.6]., and to [KM20, Pik21] for an overview of Borel graph theory. A useful observation is that if XX is a standard Borel space, then the sets [X]q[X]^{q} for q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}} and [X]<∞{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} also carry natural standard Borel structures (see §2.1), and GG is a Borel graph if and only if V⁡(G)V(G) is a standard Borel space and E⁡(G)E(G) is a Borel subset of [V⁡(G)]2[V(G)]^{2}.

Since every countable subset of a standard Borel space is Borel, countable graphs are (trivially) Borel, and hence Definition 1.2 is only really interesting when V⁡(G)V(G) is uncountable. On the other hand, a large part of descriptive combinatorics deals with the case when GG is locally countable (or even locally finite), i.e., when every vertex of GG has countably (resp. finitely) many neighbors. Indeed, all graphs considered in this paper will be locally countable. Note that GG is locally countable if and only if every connected component of GG is countable. As a result, locally countable graphs studied in descriptive combinatorics usually have uncountably many components (this is in contrast to classical, finite combinatorics, where it is common to only focus on connected graphs).

The fundamental question of descriptive combinatorics may be formulated as follows:

Question 1.3.

When can a combinatorial construction (for example, a proper qq-coloring) be performed on a Borel graph GG in a “constructive” fashion?

The word “constructive” here can mean different things depending on the context. The most basic interpretation is to require all functions, sets, etc. appearing in the construction to be Borel. By introducing additional structure on V⁡(G)V(G), this requirement may be relaxed. For instance, one may ask for a construction that is measurable with respect to a measure μ\mu on V⁡(G)V(G) or Baire-measurable with respect to a compatible Polish topology τ\tau on V⁡(G)V(G). As a concrete example, we can apply this perspective to proper colorings by modifying Definition 1.1 as follows:

Definition 1.4 (Borel, measurable, Baire-measurable chromatic numbers).

Let GG be a Borel graph. A proper qq-coloring f:V⁡(G)→qf\colon V(G)\to q of GG is Borel if f−1​(i)f^{-1}(i) is a Borel subset of V⁡(G)V(G) for all 0⩽i<q0\leqslant i<q. The Borel chromatic number χ𝖡​(G)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G) of GG is the smallest q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}} such that GG has a Borel proper qq-coloring; if no such qq exists, we set χ𝖡​(G)≔∞\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\coloneqq\infty.

Similarly, given a probability Borel measure μ\mu or a compatible Polish topology τ\tau on V⁡(G)V(G), we say that a proper qq-coloring f:V⁡(G)→qf\colon V(G)\to q of GG is μ\mu-measurable or τ\tau-Baire-measurable if f−1​(i)f^{-1}(i) is a μ\mu-measurable, resp. τ\tau-Baire-measurable subset of V⁡(G)V(G) for all 0⩽i<q0\leqslant i<q. The μ\mu-measurable chromatic number χμ​(G)\chi_{\mu}(G) and the τ\tau-Baire-measurable chromatic number χτ​(G)\chi_{\tau}(G) are defined as the smallest q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}} such that GG has a μ\mu-measurable, resp. τ\tau-Baire-measurable proper qq-coloring if such qq exists, and ∞\infty otherwise.

Definition 1.4 is due to Kechris, Solecki, and Todorcevic, who initiated the systematic study of Borel graphs and their combinatorics in the seminal paper [KST99]. Among other things, they demonstrated that greedy algorithms may be implemented on locally finite Borel graphs “in a Borel way,” leading, for instance, to the following result:

Theorem 1.5 (Kechris–Solecki–Todorcevic [KST99, Proposition 4.6]).

If GG is a Borel graph of finite maximum degree Δ\Delta, then χ𝖡​(G)⩽Δ+1\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\leqslant\Delta+1.

Unfortunately, later work revealed that without any additional assumptions, it is often impossible to improve on the initial results obtained in the Borel setting using greedy algorithms. The following theorem of Marks serves as a remarkable illustration of this, showing that the bound in Theorem 1.5 is optimal even if GG has no cycles (graphs with no cycles are called forests):

Theorem 1.6 (Marks [Mar16]).

For every Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}, there exists a Borel forest GG of maximum degree Δ\Delta such that χ𝖡​(G)=Δ+1\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)=\Delta+1.

By contrast, every forest GG satisfies χ⁡(G)⩽2\chi(G)\leqslant 2. Furthermore, Theorem 1.6 shows that the following classical upper bounds on the chromatic number fail in the Borel setting:

Theorem 1.7 (Brooks [Bro41, Die17]).

If GG is a graph of finite maximum degree Δ⩾3\Delta\geqslant 3 and without a (Δ+1)(\Delta+1)-clique, then χ⁡(G)⩽Δ\chi(G)\leqslant\Delta.

Theorem 1.8 (Johansson [Joh96, MR02]).

There exist constants CC, Δ0>0\Delta_{0}>0 such that if GG is a triangle-free graph of finite maximum degree Δ⩾Δ0\Delta\geqslant\Delta_{0}, then χ⁡(G)⩽C​Δ/log⁡Δ\chi(G)\leqslant C\Delta/\log\Delta.

Both Brooks’s and Johansson’s theorems have analogs in the measurable/Baire-measurable setting [CMT16, Ber23], showing that Marks’s Theorem 1.6 is a purely Borel phenomenon.

In view of the negative results such as Theorem 1.6, it is natural to look for additional assumptions on a Borel graph GG that improve the behavior of its Borel combinatorics. In this regard, a helpful observation is that Borel combinatorics essentially trivialize on component-finite graphs, i.e., graphs in which every connected component is finite. It is well understood in the field that a combinatorial problem admits a Borel solution on a component-finite Borel graph GG if and only if it admits any solution on GG at all (see [Pik21, §5.3] and §2.2 for two ways of making this statement precise). For example, χ𝖡​(G)=χ​(G)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)=\chi(G) for every component-finite Borel graph GG. Therefore, one may hope that Borel combinatorics on a locally countable Borel graph GG would become more approachable if GG could in some sense be “approximated” by its component-finite subgraphs.

One well-studied notion that attempts to capture this intuition is hyperfiniteness. As usual, a subgraph of a graph GG is a graph HH such that V⁡(H)⊆V⁡(G)V(H)\subseteq V(G) and E⁡(H)⊆E⁡(G)E(H)\subseteq E(G). We write H⊆GH\subseteq G to indicate that HH is a subgraph of GG. If GG and HH are Borel graphs and V⁡(H)⊆V⁡(G)V(H)\subseteq V(G) is a Borel subset equipped with the relative σ\sigma-algebra of Borel sets, we say that HH is a Borel subgraph of GG. Given a set U⊆V⁡(G)U\subseteq V(G), we let G⁡[U]G[U] denote the subgraph of GG induced by UU, i.e., the graph with vertex set UU and edge set E⁡(G⁡[U])≔E⁡(G)∩[U]2E(G[U])\coloneqq E(G)\cap[U]^{2}. Note that when U⊆V⁡(G)U\subseteq V(G) is a Borel set, G⁡[U]G[U] is a Borel subgraph of GG.

Definition 1.9 (Hyperfinite graphs).

A Borel graph GG is hyperfinite if there is an increasing sequence G0⊆G1⊆⋯⊆GG_{0}\subseteq G_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq G of component-finite Borel subgraphs of GG whose union is GG.

The systematic study of hyperfinite graphs was initiated by Weiss [Wei84] and Slaman and Steel [SS88], with important foundational work done by Dougherty, Jackson, and Kechris [DJK94] and Jackson, Kechris, and Louveau [JKL02], among others. For an overview of this topic, see [Kec21]. While hyperfiniteness is in general a very powerful notion, with many applications to measurable constructions (see, e.g., [CM16, BKS21]), counterexamples from [Con+20] show that it is largely unhelpful for obtaining Borel solutions to combinatorial problems. For example, Marks’s Theorem 1.6 remains true under the hyperfiniteness assumption:

Theorem 1.10 (Conley–Jackson–Marks–Seward–Tucker-Drob [Con+20]).

For every Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}, there exists a hyperfinite Borel forest GG of maximum degree Δ\Delta such that χ𝖡​(G)=Δ+1\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)=\Delta+1.

In particular, Theorems 1.7 and 1.8 fail in the Borel setting for hyperfinite graphs.

Nevertheless, in the breakthrough paper [Con+20a], Conley, Jackson, Marks, Seward, and Tucker-Drob succeeded in isolating a different and more subtle notion of “approximating” a graph by its component-finite subgraphs that turns out to be extremely useful in combinatorial arguments. For a graph GG and an integer R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}, GRG^{R} denotes the graph with V⁡(GR)≔V⁡(G)V(G^{R})\coloneqq V(G) in which two distinct vertices uu, vv are adjacent if and only if they are joined by a path of at most RR edges in GG.

Definition 1.11 (Asymptotic separation index).

Let GG be a Borel graph. The separation index of GG, in symbols 𝗌𝗂⁡(G)\mathsf{si}(G), is the smallest s∈ℕs\in{\mathbb{N}} for which there exists a partition V⁡(G)=U0⊔…⊔UsV(G)=U_{0}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup U_{s} of V⁡(G)V(G) into s+1s+1 Borel subsets such that the induced subgraphs G⁡[U0]G[U_{0}], …, G⁡[Us]G[U_{s}] are component-finite (if no such s∈ℕs\in{\mathbb{N}} exists, we set 𝗌𝗂⁡(G)≔∞\mathsf{si}(G)\coloneqq\infty). The asymptotic separation index of GG, in symbols 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)\mathsf{asi}(G), is the supremum of 𝗌𝗂⁡(GR)\mathsf{si}(G^{R}) taken over all R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}.

There is a growing body of literature demonstrating that various combinatorial problems admit Borel solutions on Borel graphs with finite asymptotic separation index [BW21, Con+20a, QW22, Wei21]. For example, it turns out that the Borel chromatic number of a Borel graph is bounded above by a function of its ordinary chromatic number and asymptotic separation index:

Theorem 1.12 (Conley–Jackson–Marks–Seward–Tucker-Drob [Con+20a, Theorem 8.1]).

If GG is a Borel graph with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty and χ⁡(G)<∞\chi(G)<\infty, then χ𝖡​(G)⩽(𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)+1)​χ​(G)−𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\leqslant(\mathsf{asi}(G)+1)\chi(G)-\mathsf{asi}(G).

Another example is a result of Qian and the second named author, who showed in [QW22] that a Borel graph GG of maximum degree Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}} and with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty has a Borel proper edge-coloring with Δ+1+𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)\Delta+1+\mathsf{asi}(G) colors. Moreover, if GG is bipartite, this bound can be improved to Δ+𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)\Delta+\mathsf{asi}(G) by a result of Bowen and the second named author [BW21]. (We discuss edge-colorings in more detail in §1.4.2.)

Of course, these results are only impressive assuming there is a rich family of Borel graphs with finite asymptotic separation index. Thankfully, this is indeed the case, as many natural classes of graphs have asymptotic separation index at most 11. Here is a non-exhaustive list of examples (the reader is referred to the cited papers for details and omitted definitions):

Theorem 1.13 (Conley–Jackson–Marks–Seward–Tucker-Drob [Con+20a]).

Suppose that GG is a Schreier graph of a free Borel action of a finitely generated group Γ\Gamma on a standard Borel space. Then 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)⩽1\mathsf{asi}(G)\leqslant 1, provided Γ\Gamma has at least one of the following properties:

  • —

    Γ\Gamma is virtually nilpotent;

  • —

    Γ\Gamma is polycyclic;

  • —

    Γ=ℤ2≀ℤ\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}_{2}\wr\mathbb{Z}, the lamplighter group;

  • —

    Γ=B​S​(1,2)\Gamma=BS(1,2), the Baumslag–Solitar group;

  • —

    Γ\Gamma is solvable and linear over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Theorem 1.14 (AB–Yu [BY23]).

If GG is a Borel graph of polynomial growth, then 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)⩽1\mathsf{asi}(G)\leqslant 1.

Furthermore, every locally finite Borel graph has asymptotic separation index at most 11 outside of a meager set of vertices. To state this formally, we say that a set U⊆V⁡(G)U\subseteq V(G) is GG-invariant if there are no edges between UU and V⁡(G)∖UV(G)\setminus U (i.e., if UU is a union of connected components of GG). As usual, we call a set in a topological space comeager if its complement is meager.

Theorem 1.15 (Conley–Jackson–Marks–Seward–Tucker-Drob [Con+20a, Theorem 4.8(b)]).

Let GG be a locally finite Borel graph. Fix a compatible Polish topology τ\tau on V⁡(G)V(G). Then there exists a GG-invariant comeager Borel set U⊆GU\subseteq G such that 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G⁡[U])⩽1\mathsf{asi}(G[U])\leqslant 1.

And if GG is hyperfinite, then similarly 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)⩽1\mathsf{asi}(G)\leqslant 1 on a set of full measure:

Theorem 1.16 ([Wei21a]).

Let GG be a hyperfinite locally finite Borel graph. Fix a probability Borel measure μ\mu on V⁡(G)V(G). Then there is a GG-invariant μ\mu-conull Borel set U⊆GU\subseteq G such that 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G⁡[U])⩽1\mathsf{asi}(G[U])\leqslant 1.

Both Theorems 1.15 and 1.16 are essentially present in the paper [CM16] by Conley and Miller, albeit phrased without the term “asymptotic separation index.”

It is not a coincidence that in all the above examples, the asymptotic separation index is not only finite but in fact bounded by 11: it is not known whether there exist any Borel graphs GG with 1<𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞1<\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty [Con+20a, 15]. The problem of whether such graphs exist is especially interesting in view of results such as Theorem 1.12 as well as some of our main results below.

The aim of this paper is to make several additions to the list of combinatorial constructions that can be performed in a Borel way on graphs with finite asymptotic separation index. For example, we establish a Borel version of Brooks’s Theorem 1.7 for Borel graphs GG with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty:

We also establish a Borel version of Johansson’s Theorem 1.8 for Borel graphs GG with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty. A result of this type can already be derived from Theorem 1.12. Indeed, by combining the best currently known bound on the chromatic number of triangle-free graphs (due to Molloy [Mol19]) with Theorem 1.12, we get the following result for triangle-free Borel graphs GG with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty:

χ𝖡​(G)⩽(1+ε)​(𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)+1)​Δlog⁡Δ−𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G),\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\,\leqslant\,(1+\varepsilon)(\mathsf{asi}(G)+1)\frac{\Delta}{\log\Delta}\,-\,\mathsf{asi}(G),

for any given ε>0\varepsilon>0 and large enough Δ\Delta. In other words, this approach yields a factor in front of Δ/log⁡Δ\Delta/\log\Delta that is close to 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)+1\mathsf{asi}(G)+1. We prove a bound with a factor in front of Δ/log⁡Δ\Delta/\log\Delta that is independent of 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)\mathsf{asi}(G). Furthermore, when GG has no cycles of length 33 and 44, our bound matches the best known bound on the ordinary chromatic number of GG (due to Kim [Kim95]):

It remains an interesting open question whether the 44 in the above theorem can be replaced by 11 in the triangle-free case.

While most work in descriptive combinatorics addresses specific combinatorial problems, several recent papers attack the fundamental Question 1.3 for relatively general classes of problems [Ber19, Ber21, Ber23, Ber23a, Bra+21, Csó+22, GR21, GR21a, QW22, Wei22]. We continue this line of research here by establishing a Borel version of a powerful and versatile tool from probabilistic combinatorics, the so-called Lovász Local Lemma, for Borel graphs with finite asymptotic separation index. Statements such as Theorems 1.17 and 1.18 are among the consequences of our main result, as we explain in §1.4.

1.2.  The Lovász Local Lemma and its Borel versions

Typical combinatorial problems require assigning a “color” (an element of some finite set) to every member of a given structure (e.g., to every vertex of a graph) in a way that fulfills a prescribed set of constraints. This idea is formally captured in the following definition:

Definition 1.19 (Constraint satisfaction problems).

Let qq be a positive integer. By a qq-coloring of a set SS we mean a function f:S→qf\colon S\to q.

Given a set XX and a finite subset D⊆XD\subseteq X, an (X,q)(X,q)-constraint (or simply a constraint if XX and qq are understood) with domain DD is a set B⊆qDB\subseteq q^{D} of qq-colorings of DD. If BB is a constraint with domain DD, then we write dom⁡(B)≔D\mathrm{dom}(B)\coloneqq D. We say that a qq-coloring f:X→qf\colon X\to q of XX violates a constraint BB if f|dom⁡(B)∈B{{f}|_{\mathrm{dom}(B)}}\in B, and satisfies BB otherwise.

A constraint satisfaction problem (a CSP for short) ℬ\mathscr{B} on a set XX with range qq, in symbols

ℬ:X→?q,\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q,

is a set of (X,q)(X,q)-constraints. A solution to a CSP ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q is a qq-coloring f:X→qf\colon X\to q that satisfies every constraint B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B}. We say that ℬ\mathscr{B} is satisfiable if it has a solution.

In other words, each constraint in a CSP ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q is interpreted as a set of finite “forbidden” (or “bad”) patterns that are not allowed to appear in a solution f:X→qf\colon X\to q.

Example 1.20 (Proper coloring as a CSP).

Finding a proper qq-coloring of a graph GG can be represented by a CSP ℬ:V(G)→?q\mathscr{B}\colon V(G)\to^{?}q as follows. For an edge u​v∈E⁡(G)uv\in E(G), let Bu​vB_{uv} be the constraint with domain {u,v}\{u,v\} given by Bu​v≔{(u↦i,v↦i): 0⩽i<q}B_{uv}\coloneqq\{(u\mapsto i,\,v\mapsto i)\,:\,0\leqslant i<q\}. Then a coloring f:V⁡(G)→qf\colon V(G)\to q satisfies Bu​vB_{uv} precisely when f⁡(u)≠f⁡(v)f(u)\neq f(v). Therefore, ff is a solution to ℬ≔{Bu​v:u​v∈E⁡(G)}\mathscr{B}\coloneqq\{B_{uv}\,:\,uv\in E(G)\} if and only if it is a proper qq-coloring of GG.

The Lovász Local Lemma (the LLL for short) provides a sufficient condition guaranteeing that a CSP ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q is satisfiable. To state it, we associate to ℬ\mathscr{B} two numerical parameters, 𝗉⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}) and 𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}), defined as follows. For a constraint B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B}, the probability of BB is the quantity

ℙ⁡[B]≔|B|q|dom⁡(B)|.\mathbb{P}[B]\,\coloneqq\,\frac{|B|}{q^{|\mathrm{dom}(B)|}}.

In other words, ℙ⁡[B]\mathbb{P}[B] is the probability that BB is violated by a uniformly random qq-coloring. Let

𝗉⁡(ℬ)≔supB∈ℬℙ⁡[B].\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\,\coloneqq\,\sup_{B\in\mathscr{B}}\mathbb{P}[B].

The maximum dependency degree 𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}) of ℬ\mathscr{B} is the value

𝖽⁡(ℬ)≔supB∈ℬ|{B′∈ℬ:B≠B′​ and ​dom​(B′)∩dom⁡(B)≠∅}|.\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})\,\coloneqq\,\sup_{B\in\mathscr{B}}|\{B^{\prime}\in\mathscr{B}\,:\,B\neq B^{\prime}\text{ and }\mathrm{dom}(B^{\prime})\cap\mathrm{dom}(B)\neq\varnothing\}|.
Lemma 1.21 (Lovász Local Lemma [EL75, Spe77, AS16]).

If ℬ\mathscr{B} is a CSP such that

𝗉⁡(ℬ)​(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)⩽ 1/e,\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\,(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)\,\leqslant\,1/e,

where e=2.71​…e=2.71\ldots is the base of the natural logarithm, then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a solution.

Remarks 1.22.
  1. (i)

    The statement of the LLL given above is somewhat less general than the more classical version usually found in the combinatorics literature. Specifically, the probabilities of the constraints in Lemma 1.21 are computed by considering a uniformly random qq-coloring f:X→qf\colon X\to q; that is, we view (f(x):x∈X)(f(x)\,:\,x\in X) as a collection of mutually independent discrete random variables, each distributed uniformly over a qq-element set. This specialized set-up for the LLL is called the variable version of the LLL (the name is due to Kolipaka and Szegedy [KS11]). Even though this setting is not the most general, it does encompass virtually all standard applications and is often viewed as the “right one” for algorithmic considerations (see, e.g., [Bec91, MT10, FG17]). For the statement of the LLL in abstract probability spaces, see [AS16, §5.1].

  2. (ii)

    The LLL is usually stated and proved in the case when the CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} comprises only finitely many constraints. Nevertheless, a routine compactness argument shows that an infinite CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} is satisfiable if and only if all its finite subsets ℬ′⊂ℬ\mathscr{B}^{\prime}\subset\mathscr{B} are satisfiable (see, e.g., [AS16, proof of Theorem 5.2.2]), so the conclusion of Lemma 1.21 for infinite ℬ\mathscr{B} follows from the finite case.

The LLL is used throughout combinatorics; for a sample of its applications, see [AS16, MR02].

Here we are interested in the LLL from the perspective of descriptive combinatorics. This line of research forms part of a broader program concerning versions of the LLL that are “constructive” in various senses: algorithmic [Bec91, BGR20, FG17, MT10], computable [RS14], or—as in this paper—Borel/measurable [Ber19, Ber23, Ber23a, Csó+22].

Let XX be a standard Borel space and let q∈ℕ+q\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}. Then the set 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍⁡(X,q)\mathsf{Const}(X,q) of all (X,q)(X,q)-constraints also carries a natural standard Borel structure (see §2.1), so we can define Borel CSPs as follows:

Definition 1.23 (Borel CSPs).

Let XX be a standard Borel space and let q∈ℕ+q\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}. A CSP ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q is Borel if it is a Borel subset of 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍⁡(X,q)\mathsf{Const}(X,q).

Heuristically, a CSP ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q is Borel as long as the constraints that need to be satisfied are specified “explicitly.”

Example 1.24 (Proper coloring as a Borel CSP).

If GG is a Borel graph, then the CSP from Example 1.20 that encodes proper qq-coloring problem on GG is easily seen to be Borel.

We now ask the following natural question:

Question 1.25.

Given a Borel CSP ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q on a standard Borel space XX, what LLL-style conditions guarantee that ℬ\mathscr{B} has a Borel solution f:X→qf\colon X\to q?

Without any additional assumptions on ℬ\mathscr{B}, Question 1.25 has recently been fully resolved in a series of contributions by several authors. In the following statement and in the remainder of the paper, we say that a CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} is bounded if supB∈ℬ|dom⁡(B)|<∞\sup_{B\in\mathscr{B}}|\mathrm{dom}(B)|<\infty.‡‡ ‡ The boundedness assumption can likely be removed, but it makes the results of [Ber23] easier to apply and is satisfied in most applications.

Theorem 1.26 (Brandt–Grunau–Rozhoň [BGR20], AB [Ber23], Thornton [Tho22]).

  1. (i)

    Let ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q be a bounded Borel CSP on a standard Borel space XX. If

    𝗉⁡(ℬ)​ 2𝖽⁡(ℬ)< 1,\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\,2^{\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})}\,<\,1,

    then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a Borel solution f:X→qf\colon X\to q.

  2. (ii)

    On the other hand, for every d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}}, there exists a bounded Borel CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} on a standard Borel space such that 𝖽⁡(ℬ)=d\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})=d and 𝗉⁡(ℬ)=2−d\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})=2^{-d}, so

    𝗉⁡(ℬ)​ 2𝖽⁡(ℬ)= 1,\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\,2^{\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})}\,=\,1,

    yet ℬ\mathscr{B} has no Borel solution.

Let us say a few words about how Theorem 1.26 follows from the cited sources. In [BGR20], Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň designed an efficient deterministic distributed algorithm for finding solutions to CSPs under the condition 𝗉​ 2𝖽<1\mathsf{p}\,2^{\mathsf{d}}<1 (their work builds on earlier contributions of Brandt, Maus, and Uitto [BMU19]). In [Ber23], the first named author established certain general results that allow using efficient distributed algorithms to derive conclusions in descriptive combinatorics. In particular Theorem 1.26(i) follows immediately from the Brandt–Grunau–Rozhoň algorithm via [Ber23, Theorem 2.10]. (See §1.3 for a more detailed discussion of the connections between distributed computing and descriptive combinatorics.)

The second part of Theorem 1.26 is proved by analyzing the so-called sinkless orientation problem on regular graphs. Let d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}} and let GG be a dd-regular graph. An orientation of GG is sinkless if the outdegree of every vertex is positive. A sinkless orientation of GG can be naturally encoded as a solution to a certain CSP ℬsinkless:E(G)→?2\mathscr{B}_{\text{sinkless}}\colon E(G)\to^{?}2. Here the color of each edge e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G) indicates the direction in which ee is oriented. For example, we may fix a function c:E⁡(G)→V⁡(G)c\colon E(G)\to V(G) sending each edge to one of its endpoints and say that an edge ee is oriented towards c⁡(e)c(e) if and only if its color is 00. Then we define, for each vertex vv, a constraint BvB_{v} with domain dom⁡(Bv)≔{e∈E⁡(G):e∋v}\mathrm{dom}(B_{v})\coloneqq\{e\in E(G)\,:\,e\ni v\} that requires the outdegree of vv to be positive, and let

ℬsinkless≔{Bv:v∈V⁡(G)}.\mathscr{B}_{\text{sinkless}}\,\coloneqq\,\{B_{v}\,:\,v\in V(G)\}.

Clearly, we have 𝖽⁡(ℬsinkless)=d\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}_{\text{sinkless}})=d and 𝗉⁡(ℬsinkless)=2−d\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}_{\text{sinkless}})=2^{-d}. Furthermore, if GG is a Borel graph, then the CSP ℬsinkless\mathscr{B}_{\text{sinkless}} can be made Borel by choosing a Borel function c:E⁡(G)→V⁡(G)c\colon E(G)\to V(G) using the Luzin–Novikov theorem [Kec95, Theorem 18.10]. Nevertheless, Thornton [Tho22, Theorem 3.5] applied the determinacy method of Marks [Mar16] to construct, for each d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}}, a Borel dd-regular forest GG that does not admit a Borel sinkless orientation. This verifies Theorem 1.26(ii).

While Theorem 1.26 provides a complete characterization of the range of values for the parameters 𝗉\mathsf{p} and 𝖽\mathsf{d} under which a Borel version of the LLL holds, its downside is that the inequality 𝗉​ 2𝖽<1\mathsf{p}\,2^{\mathsf{d}}<1 is much harder to satisfy than the usual LLL condition 𝗉⁡(𝖽+1)⩽1/e\mathsf{p}(\mathsf{d}+1)\leqslant 1/e. In fact, we are not aware of any applications of substantial combinatorial interest where the bound 𝗉​ 2𝖽<1\mathsf{p}\,2^{\mathsf{d}}<1 holds and Theorem 1.26(i) can be invoked. This motivates the search for other Borel versions of the LLL which make extra assumptions on the structure of the CSP in question. To formulate such assumptions, it is convenient to associate to each CSP a graph:

Definition 1.27 (Graphs associated to CSPs).

Let ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q be a CSP. Then GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} is the graph with vertex set XX in which two vertices xx, y∈Xy\in X are adjacent if and only if x≠yx\neq y and there is some constraint B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} with xx, y∈dom⁡(B)y\in\mathrm{dom}(B).

Note that if ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q is a Borel CSP and 𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}) is finite, then GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} is a locally finite Borel graph. Moreover, if additionally ℬ\mathscr{B} is bounded, then the maximum degree of GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} is finite.

An important result of Csóka, Grabowski, Máthé, Pikhurko, and Tyros is a Borel version of the LLL for CSPs whose associated graphs have subexponential growth. Here we say that a graph GG is of subexponential growth if for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there is r>0r>0 such that for all R⩾rR\geqslant r and all v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), the RR-ball around vv in GG contains at most eε​Re^{\varepsilon R} vertices.

Theorem 1.28 (Borel LLL for subexponential growth; Csóka–Grabowski–Máthé–Pikhurko–Tyros [Csó+22, Theorem 4.5]).

Let ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q be a Borel CSP on a standard Borel space XX. Suppose that the graph GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} is of subexponential growth. If

𝗉⁡(ℬ)​(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)⩽ 1/e,\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)\,\leqslant\,1/e,

then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a Borel solution f:X→qf\colon X\to q.

We investigate the situation where instead of subexponential growth, the graph GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} has finite asymptotic separation index. Actually, for our first main result, we only need an upper bound on the separation index of GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} rather than its asymptotic separation index. (Even more precisely, we use a bound on a certain auxiliary parameter closely related to 𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)\mathsf{si}(G_{\mathscr{B}}), which we call the shattering number of ℬ\mathscr{B}; see §3.1 for details.)

It is a standard observation (see, e.g., [Bec91, Ber23, CP19, FG17, GHK18]) that for a majority of applications, instead of the usual LLL condition 𝗉⁡(𝖽+1)⩽1/e\mathsf{p}(\mathsf{d}+1)\leqslant 1/e, it is enough to have a version of the LLL that holds under a polynomial criterion, i.e., with a bound of the form 𝗉​f​(𝖽)⩽1\mathsf{p}\,f(\mathsf{d})\leqslant 1 for some polynomial ff. When ss is treated as a constant parameter, our Theorem 1.29 is precisely of this type. (This should be contrasted with the exponential bound 𝗉​ 2𝖽<1\mathsf{p}\,2^{\mathsf{d}}<1 in Theorem 1.26.) For instance, if GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} has asymptotic separation index at most 11 (which happens in the numerous situations discussed in §1.1), we can apply the trivial inequality 𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)⩽𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)\mathsf{si}(G_{\mathscr{B}})\leqslant\mathsf{asi}(G_{\mathscr{B}}) to obtain the following special case of Theorem 1.29:

Most of the examples listed in Theorem 1.13 have or can have exponential growth rate. In such cases, Corollary 1.30 is an advancement over both Theorems 1.28 and 1.26(i). Interestingly, it is not known whether there exist any Borel graphs GG of subexponential growth with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)>1\mathsf{asi}(G)>1.

Of course, the result of Corollary 1.30 holds for other finite values of 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)\mathsf{asi}(G_{\mathscr{B}}) as well, but with the exponent 22 replaced by 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)+1\mathsf{asi}(G_{\mathscr{B}})+1. Our second main result is a Borel version of the LLL for bounded CSPs ℬ\mathscr{B} satisfying 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G_{\mathscr{B}})<\infty, which holds under a polynomial criterion independent of the actual value of 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)\mathsf{asi}(G_{\mathscr{B}}):

The above results add further impetus to solve the problem of whether there exist Borel graphs GG with 1<𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞1<\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty, since if they do not, Corollary 1.30 would supersede Theorem 1.31.

In addition to Borel versions of the LLL, we can also consider its measurable and Baire-measurable versions. To date, the most general result along these lines is the following:

Theorem 1.32 (AB [Ber23, Theorem 2.20]).

Let ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q be a bounded Borel CSP on a standard Borel space XX. Suppose that

𝗉⁡(ℬ)​(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)8⩽ 2−15.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\,(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)^{8}\,\leqslant\,2^{-15}.

Then the following conclusions hold:

  1. (i)

    If μ\mu is a probability Borel measure on XX, then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a μ\mu-measurable solution.

  2. (ii)

    If τ\tau is a compatible Polish topology on XX, then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a τ\tau-Baire-measurable solution.

Thus, the LLL holds measurably/Baire-measurably with a polynomial criterion. However, it is still not known whether the usual criterion 𝗉⁡(𝖽+1)⩽1/e\mathsf{p}(\mathsf{d}+1)\leqslant 1/e suffices (we conjecture that it does). By combining Corollary 1.30 with Theorem 1.15, we immediately obtain a quantitative improvement to Theorem 1.32 in the Baire-measurable case:

Similarly, if GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} is hyperfinite, Theorem 1.16 yields an improvement in the measurable setting:

1.3.  Distributed algorithms

A recent trend in descriptive combinatorics, initiated by the first named author in [Ber23], is to investigate the surprisingly intimate relationship between descriptive combinatorics and distributed computing—an area of computer science concerned with problems that can be solved efficiently by a decentralized network of processors. It turns out that the existence of an efficient distributed algorithm that solves a combinatorial problem on a class of finite graphs often implies that the same problem admits Borel, measurable, etc. solutions on certain Borel graphs [Ber23], and sometimes the reverse implication also holds [Ber23a, Bra+21, GR21a]. Using Theorem 1.29, we contribute a new result to this avenue of research, which allows using randomized distributed algorithms to solve combinatorial problems in a Borel way on graphs with finite asymptotic separation index.

The class of combinatorial problems we consider here are the so-called locally checkable labeling (LCL) problems, which were isolated by Naor and Stockmeyer in [NS95] (in [Ber23] the term “local coloring problems” is used instead). The definition of an LCL problem is very similar to the definition of a CSP given in Definition 1.19; the main difference is that an LCL problem is defined on an underlying graph using the graph’s structure:

Definition 1.35 (Locally checkable labeling problems).

A labeled graph is a pair (G,f)(G,f), where GG is a graph and f:V⁡(G)→ℕf\colon V(G)\to{\mathbb{N}} is a function, called a labeling. A rooted labeled graph is a triple (G,f,v)(G,f,v), where (G,f)(G,f) is a labeled graph and v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) is a vertex, called a root. Two rooted labeled graphs (G,f,v)(G,f,v) and (G′,f′,v′)(G^{\prime},f^{\prime},v^{\prime}) are isomorphic if there is a graph isomorphism between GG and G′G^{\prime} that sends vv to v′v^{\prime} and preserves the labeling. Given a labeled graph (G,f)(G,f), a vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), and an integer R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}, we let [G,f,v]R[G,f,v]_{R} be the isomorphism type of the rooted labeled graph

(G⁡[BG​(v,R)],f|BG​(v,R),v),\big(G[B_{G}(v,R)],\,{{f}|_{B_{G}(v,R)}},\,v\big),

where BG​(v,R)B_{G}(v,R) is the RR-ball around vv in GG.

A locally checkable labeling problem (an LCL problem for short) of radius RR is a pair Π=(R,𝒫)\Pi=(R,\mathcal{P}), where R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}} and 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a map that sends isomorphism classes of finite rooted labeled graphs to {0,1}\{0,1\}. If Π=(R,𝒫)\Pi=(R,\mathcal{P}) is an LCL problem and (G,f)(G,f) is a locally finite labeled graph, then ff solves Π\Pi on GG, or is a Π\Pi-coloring of GG, if 𝒫⁡([G,f,v]R)=1\mathcal{P}([G,f,v]_{R})=1 for all v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G). A graph GG is Π\Pi-colorable if it has a Π\Pi-coloring f:V⁡(G)→ℕf\colon V(G)\to{\mathbb{N}}.

Informally, an LCL problem Π=(R,𝒫)\Pi=(R,\mathcal{P}) is a “rule” that decides whether a labeling ff of GG is “valid” by looking at the restrictions of ff to RR-balls around individual vertices.

Example 1.36 (Proper coloring as an LCL problem).

A typical example of an LCL problem is proper qq-coloring, since whether a coloring of a graph GG is proper is determined by its restrictions to 11-balls in GG. Explicitly, given (the isomorphism type of) a finite rooted labeled graph (G,f,v)(G,f,v), set 𝒫⁡(G,f,v)≔1\mathcal{P}(G,f,v)\coloneqq 1 if and only if f⁡(v)<qf(v)<q and f⁡(u)≠f⁡(v)f(u)\neq f(v) for all neighbors uu of vv. If we let Π≔(1,𝒫)\Pi\coloneqq(1,\mathcal{P}), then a Π\Pi-coloring of a locally finite graph GG is the same as a proper qq-coloring of GG.

The model of distributed computation relevant to our work is called 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} §§ § This is not an acronym.. It was introduced by Linial in [Lin92] (although there are some earlier related results, e.g., by Alon, Babai, and Itai [ABI86], Luby [Lub86], and Goldberg, Plotkin, and Shannon [GPS88]). For an introduction to this subject, see the book [BE13] by Barenboim and Elkin.

The 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model is intended to quantify the difficulty of transforming local data into a global solution to a problem on a large (but finite!) decentralized communication network. Informally, we imagine each vertex of an nn-vertex graph GG to be occupied by a processor that may pass messages to its neighbors. The length of the messages is unrestricted, and the computational power available to each processor is unlimited (in other words, any computations carried out by individual processors take a single unit of time). Eventually, every processor must decide on its own part of the output; in the context of LCL problems, each vertex must decide on its own label. Since the processors may only communicate along the edges of GG, in TT time units, a processor can only collect information from its TT-ball in GG—this is why the model is called “𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL}”. In effect, a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm with running time TT can be thought of as a function that determines the output at each vertex of GG based only on the isomorphism type of the TT-ball around it [BE13, §4.1.2]. Formally, in addition to the graph itself, a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm also takes as input a labeling of GG, used to distinguish the vertices from each other.

Definition 1.37 (𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms).

A 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm is a function 𝒜\mathcal{A} that sends isomorphism classes of finite rooted labeled graphs to ℕ{\mathbb{N}}. Given a locally finite labeled graph (G,f)(G,f) and T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}}, the output of 𝒜\mathcal{A} on GG after time TT is the function 𝒜T​(G,f):V⁡(G)→ℕ\mathcal{A}_{T}(G,f)\colon V(G)\to{\mathbb{N}} given by

(𝒜T​(G,f))​(v)≔𝒜⁡([G,f,v]T)for all ​v∈V⁡(G).\big(\mathcal{A}_{T}(G,f)\big)(v)\,\coloneqq\,\mathcal{A}\left([G,f,v]_{T}\right)\quad\text{for all }v\in V(G).

Observe that an LCL problem, as defined in Definition 1.35, is a pair Π=(R,𝒫)\Pi=(R,\mathcal{P}) such that R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}} and 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm taking values in {0,1}\{0,1\}, and a labeling f:V⁡(G)→ℕf\colon V(G)\to{\mathbb{N}} is a Π\Pi-coloring of GG exactly when 𝒫R​(G,f)\mathcal{P}_{R}(G,f) is the constant 11 function on V⁡(G)V(G).

There are two variations of the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model, depending on the way the symmetry-breaking labeling ff in Definition 1.37 is chosen. In the deterministic version of the model, ff assigns a unique identifier to each vertex, and the output of the algorithm must provide a valid solution to the problem regardless of the specific assignment of the identifiers:

Definition 1.38 (Deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity of LCL problems).

Let Π\Pi be an LCL problem and let 𝔾\mathbb{G} be a class of finite graphs. The deterministic LOCAL\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity of Π\Pi on the class 𝔾\mathbb{G} is the function 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝔾:ℕ+→ℕ∪{∞}\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathbb{G}}\colon{\mathbb{N}}^{+}\to{\mathbb{N}}\cup\{\infty\} defined by letting 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝔾​(n)\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathbb{G}}(n) be the smallest T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}} such that there exists a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the following property:

For every nn-vertex graph G∈𝔾G\in\mathbb{G} and every bijection 𝖨𝖣:V⁡(G)→n\mathsf{ID}\colon V(G)\to n, the function 𝒜T​(G,𝖨𝖣)\mathcal{A}_{T}(G,\mathsf{ID}) is a Π\Pi-coloring of GG.

If no such T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}} exists, we set 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝔾​(n)≔∞\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathbb{G}}(n)\coloneqq\infty.

In the randomized version of the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model, the symmetry is broken using a random labeling:

Definition 1.39 (Randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity of LCL problems).

Let Π\Pi be an LCL problem and let 𝔾\mathbb{G} be a class of finite graphs. The randomized LOCAL\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity of Π\Pi on the class 𝔾\mathbb{G} is the function 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝔾:ℕ+→ℕ∪{∞}\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathbb{G}}\colon{\mathbb{N}}^{+}\to{\mathbb{N}}\cup\{\infty\} defined by letting 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝔾​(n)\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathbb{G}}(n) be the smallest T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}} such that there exist ℓ∈ℕ+\ell\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} and a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the following property:

For every nn-vertex graph G∈𝔾G\in\mathbb{G}, if a mapping ϑ:V⁡(G)→ℓ\vartheta\colon V(G)\to\ell is chosen uniformly at random, then

ℙ⁡[the function 𝒜T​(G,ϑ) is a Π-coloring of G]⩾ 1−1n.\mathbb{P}\big[\text{the function $\mathcal{A}_{T}(G,\vartheta)$ is a $\Pi$-coloring of $G$}\big]\,\geqslant\,1-\frac{1}{n}.

If no such T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}} exists, we set 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝔾​(n)≔∞\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathbb{G}}(n)\coloneqq\infty.

Unsurprisingly, the randomized version of the model is more computationally powerful than the deterministic one, and there exist many instances where a problem’s randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity is significantly lower than its deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity [CKP19].

In [Ber23], the first named author showed that fast deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms for LCL problems yield Borel solutions to these problems:¶¶ ¶ For simplicity, Theorems 1.40 and 1.41 are presented here in a somewhat less general way than the corresponding statements in [Ber23]. However, these less general formulations are sufficient for most applications. See the discussion in §3.2 and [Ber23, §2.B] for more details.

Theorem 1.40 (AB [Ber23, Theorem 2.10]).

Let Π\Pi be an LCL problem and let 𝔾\mathbb{G} be a class of Π\Pi-colorable finite graphs such that 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝔾​(n)=o⁡(log⁡n)\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathbb{G}}(n)=o(\log n). If GG is a Borel graph of finite maximum degree all of whose finite induced subgraphs are in 𝔾\mathbb{G}, then GG has a Borel Π\Pi-coloring.

Similarly, a fast randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm yields measurable/Baire-measurable solutions:

Theorem 1.41 (AB [Ber23, Theorem 2.14]).

Let Π\Pi be an LCL problem and let 𝔾\mathbb{G} be a class of Π\Pi-colorable finite graphs such that 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝔾​(n)=o⁡(log⁡n)\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathbb{G}}(n)=o(\log n). If GG is a Borel graph of finite maximum degree all of whose finite induced subgraphs are in 𝔾\mathbb{G}, then the following conclusions hold:

  1. (i)

    If μ\mu is a probability Borel measure on V⁡(G)V(G), then GG has a μ\mu-measurable Π\Pi-coloring.

  2. (ii)

    If τ\tau is a compatible Polish topology on V⁡(G)V(G), then GG has a τ\tau-Baire-measurable Π\Pi-coloring.

In other words, if we are willing to sacrifice Borelness and settle for measurable or Baire-measurable solutions, then we may use the much more powerful randomized version of the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model to find them. Here we show that if the graph GG has finite asymptotic separation index, then no sacrifice is necessary: we can obtain Borel Π\Pi-colorings of GG from randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms:

We in fact prove somewhat stronger (and numerically explicit) versions of Theorem 1.42, which are presented in §3.2. We should also note that Theorems 1.40 and 1.41 are stated in [Ber23] in the more general context of so-called structured graphs, i.e., graphs equipped with additional combinatorial data such as an orientation, a labeling, an ordering of the vertices, etc. Our results also hold for structured graphs, as we explain in §3.2.

Although it may at first seem unrelated, Theorem 1.42 is actually a relatively straightforward consequence of our main results concerning Borel versions of the LLL. As demonstrated in [Ber23], randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms and the LLL are closely linked. Specifically, [Ber23, Lemma 4.6] gives a way to reduce an LCL problem Π\Pi to an application of the LLL with a polynomial criterion using a sufficiently fast randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm. As a result, Theorem 1.42 follows in a fairly routine manner from Theorem 1.29 and [Ber23, Lemma 4.6]; the details are presented in §3.2. Curiously, the relationship between 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms and the LLL is reciprocal: in order to prove Theorem 1.31, we combine Theorem 1.42 with a fast randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm for solving instances of the LLL due to Fischer and Ghaffari [FG17] and Ghaffari, Harris, and Kuhn [GHK18]; see §3.3 for the details.

1.4.  Combinatorial applications

1.4.1.  Bounds on the Borel chromatic number

We have already mentioned two applications of our general results to the study of Borel proper colorings of graphs with finite asymptotic separation index: Theorem 1.17 (Borel version of Brooks’s theorem) and Theorem 1.18 (Borel version of Johansson’s theorem). Both of these results are derived from Theorem 1.42 by citing relevant randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms.

Proof of Theorem 1.17.

Fix an integer Δ⩾3\Delta\geqslant 3 and let 𝔹​rooksΔ\mathbb{B}\mathrm{rooks}_{\Delta} be the class of all finite graphs of maximum degree at most Δ\Delta with no (Δ+1)(\Delta+1)-cliques. Ghaffari, Hirvonen, Kuhn, and Maus [Gha+18] developed a randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm for Δ\Delta-coloring nn-vertex graphs in the class 𝔹​rooksΔ\mathbb{B}\mathrm{rooks}_{\Delta} with running time O⁡((log⁡log⁡n)2)=o⁡(log⁡n)O((\log\log n)^{2})=o(\log n). If GG is a Borel graph of maximum degree Δ\Delta and without a (Δ+1)(\Delta+1)-clique, then all its finite induced subgraphs are in 𝔹​rooksΔ\mathbb{B}\mathrm{rooks}_{\Delta}, so if 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty, then GG has a Borel proper Δ\Delta-coloring by Theorem 1.42, as desired. ∎

Theorem 1.18 is proved in exactly the same way by invoking randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms due to Chung, Pettie, and Su [CPS17]; see §4.1 for the details. As one more illustration, we show that if the Borel chromatic number of a Borel graph GG with finite asymptotic separation index is close to the maximum degree of GG, then it must be equal to the ordinary chromatic number of GG:

Proof.

Clearly, χ⁡(G)⩽χ𝖡​(G)\chi(G)\leqslant\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G). To show χ⁡(G)⩾χ𝖡​(G)\chi(G)\geqslant\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G), set q≔χ𝖡​(G)−1q\coloneqq\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)-1 and suppose, toward a contradiction, that χ⁡(G)⩽q\chi(G)\leqslant q. Let Πq\Pi_{q} be the LCL problem that encodes proper qq-coloring of graphs (see Example 1.36) and let ℂ​olΔ,q\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ol}_{\Delta,q} be the class of all finite graphs with maximum degree at most Δ\Delta and chromatic number at most qq. For large Δ\Delta and q⩾Δ−k−1q\geqslant\Delta-k-1, Bamas and Esperet [BE19, Theorem 1.3] proved that

𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Πq,ℂ​olΔ,q​(n)⩽exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡log⁡n))=o⁡(log⁡n).\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi_{q},\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ol}_{\Delta,q}}(n)\,\leqslant\,\exp(O(\sqrt{\log\log n}))\,=\,o(\log n).

Since all finite induced subgraphs of GG are in ℂ​olΔ,q\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ol}_{\Delta,q}, Theorem 1.42 implies that GG has a Borel proper qq-coloring, which contradicts the choice of qq. ∎

When Δ\Delta is sufficiently large, Theorem 1.17 is a consequence of Theorem 1.43 and Brooks’s Theorem 1.7 for the ordinary chromatic number. Similarly, we have:

Proof.

For large Δ\Delta, Reed [Ree99] showed that graphs with maximum degree Δ\Delta and without Δ\Delta-cliques have chromatic number at most Δ−1\Delta-1. Hence, the desired result follows from Theorem 1.43. ∎

1.4.2.  Borel edge-colorings

Alongside proper coloring, another classical concept in graph theory is proper edge-coloring, which is defined as follows:

Definition 1.45 (Edge-colorings and the (Borel) chromatic index).

Let GG be a graph and let q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}}. A proper qq-edge-coloring of GG is a function f:E⁡(G)→qf\colon E(G)\to q such that f⁡(e)≠f⁡(e′)f(e)\neq f(e^{\prime}) for all distinct edges ee, e′∈E⁡(G)e^{\prime}\in E(G) that share a vertex. The chromatic index χ′​(G)\chi^{\prime}(G) of GG is the smallest q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}} such that GG has a proper qq-edge-coloring; if no such q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}} exists, we set χ′​(G)≔∞\chi^{\prime}(G)\coloneqq\infty. Similarly, if GG is a Borel graph, then the Borel chromatic index χ𝖡′​(G)\chi^{\prime}_{\mathsf{B}}(G) of GG is the smallest q∈ℕq\in{\mathbb{N}} such that GG has a Borel proper qq-edge-coloring; if no such qq exists, we set χ𝖡′​(G)≔∞\chi^{\prime}_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\coloneqq\infty.

A proper qq-edge-coloring of a graph GG is exactly the same thing as a proper qq-coloring of the line graph of GG, i.e., the graph L⁡(G)L(G) with vertex set E⁡(G)E(G) and edge set {{e,e′}∈[E⁡(G)]2:|e∩e′|=1}\{\{e,e^{\prime}\}\in[E(G)]^{2}\,:\,|e\cap e^{\prime}|=1\}. If GG is a Borel graph of finite maximum degree Δ\Delta, then the maximum degree of L⁡(G)L(G) is at most 2​Δ−22\Delta-2, and hence the Borel chromatic index of GG is at most 2​Δ−12\Delta-1 by the Kechris–Solecki–Todorcevic Theorem 1.5. Marks [Mar16] proved that there exist Borel forests GG for which this bound is optimal, and Conley, Jackson, Marks, Seward, and Tucker-Drob [Con+20] further showed that such GG can be taken to be hyperfinite. The following theorem summarizes these facts:

Theorem 1.46 (Kechris–Solecki–Todorcevic [KST99, 15], Marks [Mar16, Theorem 1.4], Conley–Jackson–Marks–Seward–Tucker-Drob [Con+20, Theorem 1.4(2)]).

Fix an integer Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}.

  1. (i)

    Every Borel graph GG of maximum degree Δ\Delta satisfies χ𝖡′​(G)⩽2​Δ−1\chi^{\prime}_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\leqslant 2\Delta-1.

  2. (ii)

    There exists a hyperfinite Borel forest GG of maximum degree Δ\Delta with χ𝖡′​(G)=2​Δ−1\chi^{\prime}_{\mathsf{B}}(G)=2\Delta-1.

By contrast, a celebrated result of Vizing asserts that the ordinary chromatic index of a graph of maximum degree Δ\Delta cannot exceed Δ+1\Delta+1:

Theorem 1.47 (Vizing [Viz64]).

If GG is a graph of finite maximum degree Δ\Delta, then χ′​(G)⩽Δ+1\chi^{\prime}(G)\leqslant\Delta+1.

See [Sti+12, §A.1] for an English translation of Vizing’s paper and [BM08, Die17]for modern textbook presentations.

Theorem 1.46 precludes a Borel version of Vizing’s theorem when Δ⩾3\Delta\geqslant 3. On the other hand, a measurable version of Vizing’s theorem was recently proved by Grebík [Gre23] (building on the earlier breakthrough work of Grebík and Pikhurko [GP20]). Naturally, we would like to know what additional assumptions on GG bring the Borel chromatic index of GG closer to χ′​(G)\chi^{\prime}(G). For example, Dhawan and the first named author [BD23] showed that χ𝖡′​(G)⩽Δ+1\chi^{\prime}_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\leqslant\Delta+1 if GG is of subexponential growth. In this direction, the asymptotic separation index turns out to be an extremely helpful parameter, as demonstrated by Qian and the second named author [QW22]:

Theorem 1.48 (Qian–FW [QW22, Theorem 3.7]).

If GG is a Borel graph with finite maximum degree Δ\Delta and with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty, then χ𝖡′​(G)⩽χ′​(G)+𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}^{\prime}(G)\leqslant\chi^{\prime}(G)+\mathsf{asi}(G), and hence χ𝖡′​(G)⩽Δ+1+𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}^{\prime}(G)\leqslant\Delta+1+\mathsf{asi}(G).

In the case when GG has no odd cycles, Theorem 1.48 was established earlier by Bowen and the second named author [BW21]. Note that for graphs GG with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)⩽1\mathsf{asi}(G)\leqslant 1, examples of which are given in §1.1, Theorem 1.48 yields the bound χ𝖡′​(G)⩽Δ+2\chi_{\mathsf{B}}^{\prime}(G)\leqslant\Delta+2. It is still an open problem whether this can be reduced to Δ+1\Delta+1. It is also not known whether a bound of the form χ𝖡′​(G)⩽Δ+c\chi_{\mathsf{B}}^{\prime}(G)\leqslant\Delta+c for some fixed cc (perhaps even c=1c=1) holds for all graphs GG with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty regardless of the value of 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)\mathsf{asi}(G). As a consequence of our main results, we obtain an upper bound on χ𝖡′​(G)\chi^{\prime}_{\mathsf{B}}(G) for graphs GG with finite asymptotic separation index that is asymptotic to Δ\Delta and independent of the value of 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)\mathsf{asi}(G):

Theorem 1.49 is proved by appealing to a randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm for edge-coloring due to Chang, He, Li, Pettie, and Uitto [Cha+19]; see §4.2 for the details. In view of Theorem 1.48, Theorem 1.49 is only interesting for graphs GG whose asymptotic separation index is non-negligible compared to their maximum degree. This again highlights the importance of determining whether there exist Borel graphs GG with 1<𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞1<\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty.

1.4.3.  Borel edge-colorings of Schreier graphs

Some of the most well-studied examples in descriptive combinatorics are the so-called Schreier graphs [KM20, §6.5]. These graphs are associated to group actions and arise naturally in measurable and topological dynamics. For the remainder of §1.4.3, we fix a finitely generated group Γ\Gamma with a finite symmetric generating set F⊆Γ∖{𝟏Γ}F\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\{\mathbf{1}_{\Gamma}\}, where 𝟏Γ\mathbf{1}_{\Gamma} is the identity element of Γ\Gamma (a subset of a group is symmetric if it is closed under taking inverses). Recall that a group action 𝒂:Γ⮌X\bm{a}\colon\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is free if γ⋅𝒂x≠x\gamma\cdot_{\bm{a}}x\neq x for all x∈Xx\in X and γ∈Γ∖{𝟏Γ}\gamma\in\Gamma\setminus\{\mathbf{1}_{\Gamma}\}, i.e., if the stabilizer of every point in XX is trivial.

Definition 1.50 (Schreier graphs).

The Schreier graph of a free action 𝒂:Γ⮌X\bm{a}\colon\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is the graph 𝖲𝖼𝗁⁡(𝒂,F)\mathsf{Sch}(\bm{a},F) with vertex set XX and edge set {{x,σ⋅𝒂x}:x∈X,σ∈F}\{\{x,\sigma\cdot_{\bm{a}}x\}\,:\,x\in X,\ \sigma\in F\}.

Note that if XX is a standard Borel space and 𝒂:Γ⮌X\bm{a}\colon\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is a free Borel action (meaning that the map x↦γ⋅𝒂xx\mapsto\gamma\cdot_{\bm{a}}x is Borel for each γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma), then the corresponding Schreier graph 𝖲𝖼𝗁⁡(𝒂,F)\mathsf{Sch}(\bm{a},F) is a Borel graph of maximum degree |F||F|. In contrast to general Borel graphs, the bound in Theorem 1.46(i) is not sharp when GG is a Schreier graph, as it can be easily seen [KM20, 67] that

χ𝖡′​(𝖲𝖼𝗁⁡(𝒂,F))⩽|{σ∈F:ord⁡(σ)​ is even}|+32|{σ∈F:ord⁡(σ)​ is odd or infinite}|⩽32​|F|.\chi_{\mathsf{B}}^{\prime}(\mathsf{Sch}(\bm{a},F))\,\leqslant\,|\{\sigma\in F\,:\,\mathrm{ord}(\sigma)\text{ is even}\}|\,+\,\frac{3}{2}|\{\sigma\in F\,:\,\mathrm{ord}(\sigma)\text{ is odd or infinite}\}|\,\leqslant\,\frac{3}{2}|F|.

It is an open problem to determine the optimal upper bound on χ𝖡′​(𝖲𝖼𝗁⁡(𝒂,F))\chi_{\mathsf{B}}^{\prime}(\mathsf{Sch}(\bm{a},F)) in terms of |F||F|.

The investigation of Borel edge-colorings of Schreier graphs with finite asymptotic separation index was initiated by the second named author in [Wei21]. There it is shown that a Borel version of Vizing’s theorem holds for Schreier graphs with asymptotic separation index at most 11 under the assumption that no element of FF is of odd order (this is also a consequence of Theorem 1.48, which was proved later). Here we generalize this result by extending it to the case of arbitrary finite asymptotic separation index and allowing FF to contain elements of sufficiently large odd order:

When |F|⩽1|F|\leqslant 1, the corresponding Schreier graphs GG trivially satisfy χ𝖡′​(G)⩽|F|\chi^{\prime}_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\leqslant|F|, so there is no harm in only considering the |F|⩾2|F|\geqslant 2 case. The assumption that |F|⩾2|F|\geqslant 2 in Theorem 1.51 ensures that log⁡|F|>0\log|F|>0. We made no attempt to optimize the constant factor 2302^{30}. Note that Theorem 1.51 applies to some groups of exponential growth thanks to Theorem 1.13 (a Borel version of Vizing’s theorem for graphs of subexponential growth is already known [BD23]).

Theorem 1.51 cannot be easily derived using Theorem 1.42, because no o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n)-time randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm for Vizing’s theorem is known (although the existence of such an algorithm has not been ruled out), with the most efficient currently available algorithm running in time O⁡(log2⁡n)O(\log^{2}n) [BD23a]. Instead, we prove Theorem 1.51 by invoking our Borel LLL (i.e., Theorem 1.31) directly. More precisely, we apply Theorem 1.31 to prove a certain general result about Borel independent complete sections, which is described in §1.4.4, and then use it to deduce Theorem 1.51.

1.4.4.  Borel independent complete sections

For a graph GG, a set I⊆V⁡(G)I\subseteq V(G) is GG-independent if no two vertices in II are adjacent. If ℱ\mathcal{F} is a family of pairwise disjoint sets, then a complete section for ℱ\mathcal{F} is a set SS that includes at least one element from every set in ℱ\mathcal{F}. The following classical fact is proved by a simple application of the LLL:

Theorem 1.52 (Alon [Alo88, Alo94, AS16]).

Let GG be a graph of finite maximum degree Δ\Delta and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a family of pairwise disjoint subsets of V⁡(G)V(G). If |S|⩾2​e​Δ|S|\geqslant 2e\Delta for all S∈ℱS\in\mathcal{F}, then there is a GG-independent complete section for ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Theorem 1.52, and independent complete sections in general, have been a subject of considerable interest, not least because of their many applications to other combinatorial problems.∥∥ ∥ A related notion considered in the literature is that of an independent transversal—i.e., a set that meets each member of ℱ\mathcal{F} in exactly one point. For our purposes, working with complete sections will be more natural. Note that the existence of a GG-independent complete section for ℱ\mathcal{F} is equivalent to the existence of a GG-independent transversal (although this equivalence may fail in the Borel setting). The required lower bound on the sizes of the sets in ℱ\mathcal{F} has been subsequently improved from 2​e​Δ2e\Delta to 2​Δ2\Delta by Haxell [Hax01], which is best possible [BES75].

We prove a Borel version of Theorem 1.52 under a finite asymptotic separation index assumption. To simplify the statement of our result, we say that a set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is a complete section for a graph GG if it meets every connected component of GG. In other words, SS is a complete section for GG if and only if it is a complete section for the following family of sets:

ℱ≔{V⁡(C):C is a connected component of G}.\mathcal{F}\,\coloneqq\,\{V(C)\,:\,\text{$C$ is a connected component of $G$}\}.

A subgraph G′G^{\prime} of GG is spanning if V⁡(G′)=V⁡(G)V(G^{\prime})=V(G).

The assumption that 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(H)<∞\mathsf{asi}(H)<\infty in Theorem 1.53 cannot be removed. Indeed, Marks [Mar16, Theorem 1.6] gave an example of a Borel graph HH and two spanning Borel subgraphs G1G_{1}, G2G_{2} such that both G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} have maximum degree 22, all their components are infinite, and every Borel set A⊆V⁡(H)A\subseteq V(H) either includes an entire component of G1G_{1} (and hence it is definitely not G1G_{1}-independent), or misses a component of G2G_{2} (i.e., it is not a complete section for G2G_{2}).

The usual proof of Theorem 1.52 is one of the rare applications of the LLL for which the bound 𝗉⁡(𝖽+1)⩽1/e\mathsf{p}(\mathsf{d}+1)\leqslant 1/e is sharp and a polynomial criterion is insufficient. As a result, we cannot establish Theorem 1.53 by simply following the standard proof of Theorem 1.52 and substituting Theorem 1.29 or Theorem 1.31 in place of the LLL. Nevertheless, we are able to prove Theorem 1.53 using a different approach, which unfortunately results in a superlinear lower bound on the size of the components of G2G_{2}. However, we suspect that the conclusion of Theorem 1.53 should hold even if the components of G2G_{2} have size bounded below by some linear function of Δ\Delta:

Conjecture 1.54.

There exist constants CC, Δ0>0\Delta_{0}>0 with the following property: Let HH be a Borel graph with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(H)<∞\mathsf{asi}(H)<\infty and let G1G_{1}, G2G_{2} be two spanning Borel subgraphs of HH. Suppose that the maximum degree of G1G_{1} is at most Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}, where Δ⩾Δ0\Delta\geqslant\Delta_{0}. If every component of G2G_{2} contains at least C​ΔC\Delta vertices, then there is a Borel G1G_{1}-independent complete section for G2G_{2}.

One way to settle Conjecture 1.54 would be to prove a version of Theorem 1.31 under the usual LLL assumption 𝗉⁡(𝖽+1)⩽1/e\mathsf{p}(\mathsf{d}+1)\leqslant 1/e. Since we suspect that Δ​log⁡Δ\Delta\log\Delta is not the optimal order of magnitude in Theorem 1.53, we made no attempt to optimize the constant factor 2252^{25}. We prove Theorem 1.53 in §4.3 and then use it to derive Theorem 1.51 in §4.4. If Conjecture 1.54 is true, then the same argument would improve Theorem 1.51 by replacing the bound 230​|F|​log⁡|F|2^{30}\,|F|\log|F| by a linear function of |F||F|. We expect that this can also be achieved by following a “nibbling” approach similar to the one in the paper [RS02] by Reed and Sudakov, but the resulting argument would be quite technical, and since we do not see how to generalize it to prove Conjecture 1.54 in full, we do not pursue it in this paper.

2.  Preliminaries

2.1.  The spaces of finite sets and constraints

In this subsection, given a standard Borel space XX and an integer q∈ℕ+q\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}, we describe a way of endowing the set 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍⁡(X,q)\mathsf{Const}(X,q) of all (X,q)(X,q)-constraints with the structure of a standard Borel space (this is necessary for Definition 1.23 to make sense). The material in this subsection is entirely standard; nevertheless, we decided to include it here for completeness.

Let XX be a standard Borel space. We begin by equipping [X]k[X]^{k} for k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} with the structure of a standard Borel space. To this end, let (X)k(X)^{k} be the set of all kk-tuples (x0,…,xk−1)∈Xk(x_{0},\ldots,x_{k-1})\in X^{k} of distinct points, and let ∼k\sim_{k} be the equivalence relation on (X)k(X)^{k} given by

(x0,…,xk−1)∼k(y0,…,yk−1):⟺{x0,…,xk−1}={y0,…,yk−1}.(x_{0},\ldots,x_{k-1})\,\sim_{k}\,(y_{0},\ldots,y_{k-1})\quad\vcentcolon\Longleftrightarrow\quad\{x_{0},\ldots,x_{k-1}\}\,=\,\{y_{0},\ldots,y_{k-1}\}.

By [KM04, Example 6.1 and Proposition 6.3], the quotient space [X]k=(X)k/∼k[X]^{k}=(X)^{k}/\sim_{k} is standard Borel. It follows that the disjoint union [X]<∞=[X]0⊔[X]1⊔[X]2⊔…{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}}=[X]^{0}\sqcup[X]^{1}\sqcup[X]^{2}\sqcup\ldots is standard Borel as well [Tse16, Proposition 1.4].

Next, given q∈ℕ+q\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}, we let [X⇢q]<∞{[{{X}\dashrightarrow{q}}]^{{<\infty}}} be the set of all partial functions φ:X⇢q\varphi\colon X\dashrightarrow q such that dom⁡(φ)\mathrm{dom}(\varphi) is a finite subset of XX. Each φ∈[X⇢q]<∞\varphi\in{[{{X}\dashrightarrow{q}}]^{{<\infty}}} can be identified with a finite subset of X×qX\times q, namely, with its graph {(x,φ⁡(x)):x∈dom⁡(φ)}\{(x,\varphi(x))\,:\,x\in\mathrm{dom}(\varphi)\}. Using this identification, it is routine to check that [X⇢q]<∞{[{{X}\dashrightarrow{q}}]^{{<\infty}}} is a Borel subset of [X×q]<∞{[{{X\times q}}]^{{<\infty}}}.

Finally, since an (X,q)(X,q)-constraint is a finite subset of [X⇢q]<∞{[{{X}\dashrightarrow{q}}]^{{<\infty}}}, we may define

𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍(X,q)≔{B∈[[X⇢q]<∞]<∞:all functions in B have the same domain}.\mathsf{Const}(X,q)\,\coloneqq\,\big\{B\in{[{{{[{{X}\dashrightarrow{q}}]^{{<\infty}}}}}]^{{<\infty}}}\,:\,\text{all functions in $B$ have the same domain}\big\}.

It can be easily verified that 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍⁡(X,q)\mathsf{Const}(X,q) is a Borel subset of the standard Borel space [[X⇢q]<∞]<∞{[{{{[{{X}\dashrightarrow{q}}]^{{<\infty}}}}}]^{{<\infty}}}, and therefore, equipped with the relative σ\sigma-algebra of Borel sets, it is also standard Borel.

2.2.  Borel combinatorics on component-finite graphs

As mentioned in the introduction, the reason we expect graphs with finite asymptotic separation index to have well-behaved Borel combinatorics is that Borel combinatorics “trivialize” on component-finite graphs. The following statement makes this intuition rigorous:

Proposition 2.1 (Borel combinatorics on component-finite graphs).

Let ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q be a Borel CSP on a standard Borel space XX. If the graph GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} is component-finite and ℬ\mathscr{B} has a solution, then it has a Borel solution as well.

The proof of Proposition 2.1 relies on the following deep and classical result (which we shall use throughout the paper without mention):

Theorem 2.2 (Luzin–Novikov uniformization [Kec95, Theorem 18.10]).

Let XX, YY be standard Borel spaces and let R⊆X×YR\subseteq X\times Y be a Borel subset. If for every x∈Xx\in X, the set

Rx≔{y∈Y:(x,y)∈R}R_{x}\,\coloneqq\,\{y\in Y\,:\,(x,y)\in R\}

is countable, then there exists a sequence (fn)n∈ℕ(f_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} of Borel partial functions fn:X⇢Yf_{n}\colon X\dashrightarrow Y defined on Borel subsets of XX such that for all x∈Xx\in X, Rx={fn(x):n∈ℕ,x∈dom(fn)}R_{x}=\{f_{n}(x)\,:\,n\in{\mathbb{N}},\ x\in\mathrm{dom}(f_{n})\}.

If additionally each set RxR_{x} is nonempty, then the mapping f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y given by

f⁡(x)≔fn⁡(x)​(x), where ​n​(x)≔min⁡{n∈ℕ:x∈dom⁡(fn)},f(x)\,\coloneqq\,f_{n(x)}(x),\text{ where }n(x)\,\coloneqq\,\min\{n\in{\mathbb{N}}\,:\,x\in\mathrm{dom}(f_{n})\},

is a Borel function such that f⁡(x)∈Rxf(x)\in R_{x} for all x∈Xx\in X.

Proof of Proposition 2.1.

This is a standard argument in descriptive combinatorics, so we only provide a proof sketch. Roughly, since on each component of GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} the problem can be solved in only finitely many ways, the Luzin–Novikov theorem yields a Borel choice of one solution on every component; putting the chosen solutions together solves the problem on the whole space.

In a little more detail, let 𝒞≔{V⁡(C):C is a connected component of Gℬ}\mathcal{C}\coloneqq\{V(C)\,:\,\text{$C$ is a connected component of $G_{\mathscr{B}}$}\}. This is a Borel subset of [X]<∞{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}}. Say that a finite partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} is a map φ∈[X⇢q]<∞\varphi\in{[{{X}\dashrightarrow{q}}]^{{<\infty}}} such that φ\varphi satisfies every constraint B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} with dom⁡(B)⊆dom⁡(φ)\mathrm{dom}(B)\subseteq\mathrm{dom}(\varphi). Then the set 𝒮⊆[X⇢q]<∞\mathcal{S}\subseteq{[{{X}\dashrightarrow{q}}]^{{<\infty}}} of all finite partial solutions to ℬ\mathscr{B} is also Borel. Since ℬ\mathscr{B} has a solution, for each finite set U⊆XU\subseteq X, there is some φ∈𝒮\varphi\in\mathcal{S} with dom⁡(φ)=U\mathrm{dom}(\varphi)=U. Let

R≔{(U,φ)∈𝒞×𝒮:dom⁡(φ)=U}.R\,\coloneqq\,\{(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{S}\,:\,\mathrm{dom}(\varphi)=U\}.

Then RR is a Borel subset of 𝒞×𝒮\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{S}, and for each U∈𝒞U\in\mathcal{C}, the set RU≔{φ∈𝒮:(U,φ)∈R}R_{U}\coloneqq\{\varphi\in\mathcal{S}\,:\,(U,\varphi)\in R\} is finite and nonempty. Therefore, by the Luzin–Novikov theorem (Theorem 2.2), there exists a Borel function 𝒞→𝒮:U↦φU\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{S}\colon U\mapsto\varphi_{U} such that dom⁡(φU)=U\mathrm{dom}(\varphi_{U})=U for all UU. For each x∈Xx\in X, let [x]∈𝒞[x]\in\mathcal{C} be the vertex set of the component containing xx. Then the map f:X→qf\colon X\to q given by

f⁡(x)≔φ[x]​(x)for all ​x∈X,f(x)\,\coloneqq\,\varphi_{[x]}(x)\quad\text{for all }x\in X,

or, equivalently, f≔⨆U∈𝒞φUf\coloneqq\bigsqcup_{U\in\mathcal{C}}\varphi_{U}, is a Borel solution to ℬ\mathscr{B}, as desired. ∎

Corollary 2.3.

If GG is a component-finite Borel graph and χ⁡(G)<∞\chi(G)<\infty, then χ𝖡​(G)=χ​(G)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)=\chi(G).

Proof.

Clearly, χ𝖡​(G)⩾χ⁡(G)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\geqslant\chi(G). To see that χ𝖡​(G)⩽χ⁡(G)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\leqslant\chi(G), recall from Example 1.24 that the proper χ⁡(G)\chi(G)-coloring problem for GG can be encoded via a Borel CSP ℬ:V(G)→?χ(G)\mathscr{B}\colon V(G)\to^{?}\chi(G) given by

ℬ≔{{(u↦i,v↦i): 0⩽i<χ(G)}:uv∈E(G)}.\mathscr{B}\,\coloneqq\,\big\{\{(u\mapsto i,\,v\mapsto i)\,:\,0\leqslant i<\chi(G)\}\,:\,uv\in E(G)\}.

Since Gℬ=GG_{\mathscr{B}}=G is component-finite, it has a Borel proper χ⁡(G)\chi(G)-coloring by Proposition 2.1. ∎

Another useful consequence of the Luzin–Novikov theorem is the fact that if f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y is a countable-to-one Borel function between standard Borel spaces, then its image f⁡(X)f(X) is a Borel subset of YY [Kec95, Exercise 18.14].

3.  Proofs of the main results

3.1.  Proof of Theorem 1.29

As stated in §1.2, in our proof of Theorem 1.29 we will use an auxiliary parameter in place of the separation index. The following definition is reminiscent of (and inspired by) an alternative way of defining asymptotic separation index given in [Con+20a, Lemma 3.1(1’)].

Definition 3.1 (Shattering number).

Let ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q be a Borel CSP on a standard Borel space XX. The shattering number of ℬ\mathscr{B}, denoted by 𝗌𝗁⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{sh}(\mathscr{B}), is the smallest s∈ℕs\in{\mathbb{N}} for which there exists a Borel family 𝒫⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{P}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} of finite subsets of XX such that 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a partition of XX and for each B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B}, dom⁡(B)\mathrm{dom}(B) intersects at most ss members of 𝒫\mathcal{P} (if no such s∈ℕs\in{\mathbb{N}} exists, we set 𝗌𝗁⁡(ℬ)≔∞\mathsf{sh}(\mathscr{B})\coloneqq\infty).

Some readers may be more familiar with describing a partition of a standard Borel space XX into finite sets as an equivalence relation on XX with finite classes. For their benefit, we remark that a partition 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a Borel subset of [X]<∞{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} if and only if the equivalence relation whose classes are the members of 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a Borel subset of X2X^{2} [BY23, Lemma 3.8].

Let us observe two easy upper bounds on the shattering number of a Borel CSP.

Lemma 3.2.

If ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q be a Borel CSP on a standard Borel space XX, then:

  1. (i)

    𝗌𝗁⁡(ℬ)⩽𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)+1\mathsf{sh}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant\mathsf{si}(G_{\mathscr{B}})+1, and

  2. (ii)

    𝗌𝗁⁡(ℬ)⩽supB∈ℬ|dom⁡(B)|\mathsf{sh}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant\sup_{B\in\mathscr{B}}|\mathrm{dom}(B)|.

Proof.

For (i), suppose that X=U0⊔…⊔UsX=U_{0}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup U_{s} is a partition witnessing 𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)=s\mathsf{si}(G_{\mathscr{B}})=s. Then

𝒫≔{V⁡(C):C is a connected component of G⁡[Ui] for some 0⩽i⩽s}\mathcal{P}\,\coloneqq\,\{V(C)\,:\,\text{$C$ is a connected component of $G[U_{i}]$ for some $0\leqslant i\leqslant s$}\}

is a family of finite sets witnessing 𝗌𝗁⁡(ℬ)⩽s+1\mathsf{sh}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant s+1. For (ii), take 𝒫={{x}:x∈X}\mathcal{P}=\{\{x\}\,:\,x\in X\}. ∎

We can now state the strengthening of Theorem 1.29 using the shattering number:

Theorem 1.29 is a direct consequence of Theorem 3.3 and Lemma 3.2(i). On the other hand, combining Theorem 3.3 with Lemma 3.2(ii) gives a conclusion reminiscent of, though slightly weaker than, [Ber23a, Corollary 1.8].

The technique we employ to prove Theorem 3.3 is known as the method of conditional probabilities in computer science, where it is commonly used for derandomization [AS16, MR95]. This method has already been applied to obtain “constructive” versions of the LLL, for instance by Beck [Bec91], Fischer and Ghaffari [FG17], and the first named author [Ber23a]. We especially highlight the connection to [FG17, Theorem 3.6] by Fischer and Ghaffari, which uses so-called network decompositions to design efficient distributed algorithms in a way that is rather analogous to our use of the shattering number.

Our proof of Theorem 3.3 is inductive: we shall construct the desired qq-coloring of XX that solves ℬ\mathscr{B} by iteratively coloring subsets of XX. Throughout the iterations, the domains of the constraints will be shrinking until they become empty. Note that there are precisely two constraints with the empty domain: ∅\varnothing and {∅}\{\varnothing\}. The constraint {∅}\{\varnothing\} has probability 1/q0=11/q^{0}=1 and is violated by every coloring, while the constraint ∅\varnothing has probability 00 and is always satisfied. The distinction between these two cases will play a decisive role in the last stage of our proof.

To facilitate the analysis of the iterative process, the following notation will be useful. Fix a set XX and an integer q∈ℕ+q\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} and let f:U→qf\colon U\to q be a qq-coloring of a subset U⊆XU\subseteq X. For an (X,q)(X,q)-constraint BB, we write B/fB/f to denote the constraint with dom⁡(B/f)≔dom⁡(B)∖U\mathrm{dom}(B/f)\coloneqq\mathrm{dom}(B)\setminus U given by

B/f≔{φ:(dom(B)∖U)→q:f|dom⁡(B)∩U⊔φ∈B}.B/f\,\coloneqq\,\{\varphi\colon(\mathrm{dom}(B)\setminus U)\to q\,:\,{{f}|_{\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U}}\,\sqcup\,\varphi\,\in\,B\}.

In other words, φ∈B/f\varphi\in B/f if and only if the coloring f⊔φf\sqcup\varphi violates BB. We emphasize that it is possible to have dom⁡(B)⊆U\mathrm{dom}(B)\subseteq U, in which case dom⁡(B/f)=∅\mathrm{dom}(B/f)=\varnothing. More specifically, if dom⁡(B)⊆U\mathrm{dom}(B)\subseteq U, then

B/f={{∅}if f violates B;∅if f satisfies B.B/f\,=\,\begin{cases}\{\varnothing\}&\text{if $f$ violates $B$};\\ \varnothing&\text{if $f$ satisfies $B$}.\end{cases}

Observe that if f′:U′→qf^{\prime}\colon U^{\prime}\to q is another qq-coloring of some set U′⊆X∖UU^{\prime}\subseteq X\setminus U, then

(B/f)/f′=B/(f⊔f′).(B/f)/f^{\prime}\,=\,B/(f\sqcup f^{\prime}).

Given a CSP ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q, we define a CSP ℬ/f:(X∖U)→?q\mathscr{B}/f\colon(X\setminus U)\to^{?}q by

ℬ/f≔{B/f:B∈ℬ}.\mathscr{B}/f\,\coloneqq\,\{B/f\,:\,B\in\mathscr{B}\}.

By construction, f′:(X∖U)→qf^{\prime}\colon(X\setminus U)\to q is a solution to ℬ/f\mathscr{B}/f if and only if f⊔f′f\sqcup f^{\prime} is a solution to ℬ\mathscr{B}. Note that we always have 𝖽⁡(ℬ/f)⩽𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}/f)\leqslant\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}), but there is no a priori relation between 𝗉⁡(ℬ/f)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}/f) and 𝗉⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}).

The following lemma describes the inductive step in the proof of Theorem 3.3:

Lemma 3.4.

Let ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q be a Borel CSP on a standard Borel space XX and let s:ℬ→ℕs\colon\mathscr{B}\to{\mathbb{N}} be a Borel function such that for all B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B},

(3.2) ℙ⁡[B]​(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)s⁡(B)<e−s⁡(B).\mathbb{P}[B]\,(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)^{s(B)}\,<\,e^{-s(B)}.

Let U⊆XU\subseteq X be a Borel set such that the graph Gℬ​[U]G_{\mathscr{B}}[U] is component-finite. For each B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B}, define

η⁡(B)≔{1if dom⁡(B)∩U≠∅;0otherwise.\eta(B)\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}1&\text{if $\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U\neq\varnothing$};\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Then there exists a Borel function f:U→qf\colon U\to q such that for all B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B},

(3.3) ℙ⁡[B/f]​(𝖽⁡(ℬ/f)+1)s⁡(B)−η⁡(B)<e−s⁡(B)+η⁡(B).\mathbb{P}[B/f]\,(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}/f)+1)^{s(B)-\eta(B)}\,<\,e^{-s(B)+\eta(B)}.
Proof.

Note that if B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} is a constraint such that dom⁡(B)∩U=∅\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U=\varnothing, then (3.3) holds for this BB regardless of the choice of f:U→qf\colon U\to q, since B/f=BB/f=B, 𝖽⁡(ℬ/f)⩽𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}/f)\leqslant\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}), and η⁡(B)=0\eta(B)=0. Therefore, we only need to focus on the constraints B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} with dom⁡(B)∩U≠∅\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U\neq\varnothing. Consider any such constraint BB. For a function ψ:(dom⁡(B)∩U)→q\psi\colon(\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U)\to q, let the probability of BB conditioned on ψ\psi be

ℙ[B|ψ]≔|{φ∈B:φ|dom⁡(B)∩U=ψ}|q|dom⁡(B)∖U|.\mathbb{P}[B\,|\,\psi]\,\coloneqq\,\frac{|\{\varphi\in B\,:\,{{\varphi}|_{\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U}}=\psi\}|}{q^{|\mathrm{dom}(B)\setminus U|}}.

In other words, ℙ⁡[B|ψ]\mathbb{P}[B\,|\,\psi] is the probability that a uniformly random qq-coloring of dom⁡(B)\mathrm{dom}(B) violates BB given that it agrees with ψ\psi on dom⁡(B)∩U\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U. Observe that for any f:U→qf\colon U\to q, we have

(3.4) ℙ⁡[B/f]=ℙ⁡[B​|f|dom⁡(B)∩U].\mathbb{P}[B/f]\,=\,\mathbb{P}[B\,|\,{{f}|_{\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U}}].

Let B∗B^{\ast} be the constraint with dom⁡(B∗)≔dom⁡(B)∩U\mathrm{dom}(B^{\ast})\coloneqq\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U given by

B∗≔{ψ:(dom(B)∩U)→q:ℙ[B|ψ]⩾(e(𝖽(ℬ)+1))−s⁡(B)+1}.B^{\ast}\,\coloneqq\,\big\{\psi\colon(\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U)\to q\ :\ \mathbb{P}[B\,|\,\psi]\,\geqslant\,(e(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1))^{-s(B)+1}\big\}.

Simple double counting shows that

(e(𝖽(ℬ)+1))−s⁡(B)>(3.2)ℙ[B]=q−|dom⁡(B)∩U|∑ψ:(dom⁡(B)∩U)→qℙ[B|ψ]\displaystyle(e(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1))^{-s(B)}\,\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\eqref{eq:key_lemma_assumption}}}}{{>}}\,\mathbb{P}[B]\,=\,q^{-|\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U|}\sum_{\psi\colon(\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U)\to q}\mathbb{P}[B\,|\,\psi]
⩾q−|dom⁡(B)∩U||B∗|(e⁡(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1))−s⁡(B)+1=ℙ⁡[B∗]​(e⁡(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1))−s⁡(B)+1.\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\geqslant\,q^{-|\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U|}\,|B^{\ast}|\,(e(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1))^{-s(B)+1}\,=\,\mathbb{P}[B^{\ast}]\,(e(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1))^{-s(B)+1}.

(This is essentially Markov’s inequality from probability theory.) We conclude that

(3.5) ℙ⁡[B∗]​(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)< 1/e.\mathbb{P}[B^{\ast}]\,(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)\,<\,1/e.

Now let ℬ∗:U→?q\mathscr{B}^{\ast}\colon U\to^{?}q be the Borel CSP defined by

ℬ∗≔{B∗:B∈ℬ,dom(B)∩U≠∅}.\mathscr{B}^{\ast}\,\coloneqq\,\{B^{\ast}\,:\,B\in\mathscr{B},\ \mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U\neq\varnothing\}.

Since 𝖽⁡(ℬ∗)⩽𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}^{\ast})\leqslant\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}) by construction, it follows from (3.5) that ℬ\mathscr{B} satisfies the assumptions of the ordinary LLL, i.e., of Lemma 1.21. Therefore, ℬ∗\mathscr{B}^{\ast} has a solution. Note that Gℬ∗=Gℬ​[U]G_{\mathscr{B}^{\ast}}=G_{\mathscr{B}}[U], which is component-finite by hypothesis. Thus, ℬ∗\mathscr{B}^{\ast} has a Borel solution f:U→qf\colon U\to q by Proposition 2.1. We conclude from (3.4), the definition of ℬ∗\mathscr{B}^{\ast}, and the inequality 𝖽⁡(ℬ/f)⩽𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}/f)\leqslant\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}) that ff is as desired. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.3.

Let 𝒫⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{P}\subseteq[X]^{<\infty} be a Borel family of finite sets witnessing that 𝗌𝗁⁡(ℬ)⩽s\mathsf{sh}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant s. We claim there exists a partition 𝒫=⨆n∈ℕ𝒫n\mathcal{P}=\bigsqcup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}\mathcal{P}_{n} of 𝒫\mathcal{P} into countably many Borel sets such that for each B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} and n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, dom⁡(B)\mathrm{dom}(B) meets at most one member of 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}.
