Indeed, let HH be the Borel graph with vertex set 𝒫\mathcal{P} in which distinct sets SS, R∈𝒫R\in\mathcal{P} are adjacent if and only if there is a constraint B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} such that dom⁡(B)\mathrm{dom}(B) meets both SS and RR. Each set S∈𝒫S\in\mathcal{P} is finite, and every point in SS belongs to at most 𝖽⁡(ℬ)<∞\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})<\infty constraints in ℬ\mathscr{B} (𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}) is finite by (3.1)). Since every constraint intersects finitely many sets in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, it follows that the graph HH is locally finite. Therefore, by [KST99, Proposition 4.5], there is a Borel function c:𝒫→ℕc\colon\mathcal{P}\to{\mathbb{N}} such that c⁡(S)≠c⁡(R)c(S)\neq c(R) whenever SS and RR are adjacent in HH (i.e., cc is a Borel proper ℕ{\mathbb{N}}-coloring of HH). Setting 𝒫n≔c−1​(n)\mathcal{P}_{n}\coloneqq c^{-1}(n) gives the desired partition of 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

For n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, let Un≔⋃𝒫nU_{n}\coloneqq\bigcup\mathcal{P}_{n}, so X=⨆n∈ℕUnX=\bigsqcup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}U_{n} is a partition of XX into Borel sets. For each n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, each connected component of Gℬ​[Un]G_{\mathscr{B}}[U_{n}] is contained in an element of 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}, and so Gℬ​[Un]G_{\mathscr{B}}[U_{n}] is component-finite. For each B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} and n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, let tn​(B)t_{n}(B) be the number of sets UiU_{i} with i<ni<n such that dom⁡(B)∩Ui≠∅\mathrm{dom}(B)\cap U_{i}\neq\varnothing and set sn​(B)≔s−tn​(B)s_{n}(B)\coloneqq s-t_{n}(B) (thus, t0​(B)=0t_{0}(B)=0 and s0​(B)=ss_{0}(B)=s). By assumption, tn​(B)⩽st_{n}(B)\leqslant s for all n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and thus sn​(B)⩾0s_{n}(B)\geqslant 0. Hypothesis (3.1) yields

ℙ⁡[B]​(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)s0​(B)⩽e−s0​(B)for all ​B∈ℬ.\mathbb{P}[B]\,(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)^{s_{0}(B)}\,\leqslant\,e^{-s_{0}(B)}\quad\text{for all }B\in\mathscr{B}.

In fact, this inequality is strict, since its left-hand side is rational, while its right-hand side is not. We may now set B(0)≔BB^{(0)}\coloneqq B for all B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} and ℬ(0)≔ℬ\mathscr{B}^{(0)}\coloneqq\mathscr{B} and then iteratively apply Lemma 3.4 to produce a sequence of Borel qq-colorings fn:Un→qf_{n}\colon U_{n}\to q such that for each n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B},

(3.6) ℙ⁡[B(n+1)]​(𝖽⁡(ℬ(n+1))+1)sn+1​(B)<e−sn+1​(B),\mathbb{P}[B^{(n+1)}]\,(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}^{(n+1)})+1)^{s_{n+1}(B)}\,<\,e^{-s_{n+1}(B)},

where B(n+1)≔B/(f0⊔…⊔fn)=B(n)/fnB^{(n+1)}\coloneqq B/(f_{0}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup f_{n})=B^{(n)}/f_{n} and ℬ(n+1)≔ℬ/(f0⊔…⊔fn)=ℬ(n)/fn\mathscr{B}^{(n+1)}\coloneqq\mathscr{B}/(f_{0}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup f_{n})=\mathscr{B}^{(n)}/f_{n}. We claim that the Borel function f≔⨆n∈ℕfnf\coloneqq\bigsqcup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}f_{n} is a solution to ℬ\mathscr{B}. Indeed, consider any constraint B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B}. To see that ff satisfies BB, note that since dom⁡(B)\mathrm{dom}(B) if finite, there is some n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} such that

f|dom⁡(B)=(f0⊔…⊔fn)|dom⁡(B).{{f}|_{\mathrm{dom}(B)}}\,=\,{{(f_{0}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup f_{n})}|_{\mathrm{dom}(B)}}.

ℙ⁡[B/f]=ℙ⁡[B/(f0⊔…⊔fn)]=ℙ⁡[B(n+1)]<(e⁡(𝖽⁡(ℬ(n+1))+1))−sn+1​(B)⩽ 1.\mathbb{P}[B/f]\,=\,\mathbb{P}[B/(f_{0}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup f_{n})]\,=\,\mathbb{P}[B^{(n+1)}]\,<\,(e(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}^{(n+1)})+1))^{-s_{n+1}(B)}\,\leqslant\,1.

Since dom⁡(B/f)=∅\mathrm{dom}(B/f)=\varnothing, it follows that B/f=∅B/f=\varnothing, i.e., ff satisfies BB, as desired. ∎

3.2.  From the LLL to LOCAL\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms

As briefly mentioned in the introduction, LCL problems and 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms can be defined in the situation when the underlying graph is equipped with additional combinatorial structure, such as an orientation, a labeling, etc. Since we will need this general set-up for the proof of Theorem 1.31, we recall the necessary definitions here. Our presentation follows that in [Ber23, §2.A].

For a set XX, let X<∞≔X0⊔X1⊔X2⊔…X^{<\infty}\coloneqq X^{0}\sqcup X^{1}\sqcup X^{2}\sqcup\ldots be the set of all finite tuples of elements of XX.

Definition 3.5 (Structured graphs).

Let GG be a graph. A structure map on GG is a partial function σ:V​(G)<∞⇢ℕ\sigma\colon V(G)^{<\infty}\dashrightarrow{\mathbb{N}} such that for some ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in{\mathbb{N}}, every tuple 𝒙∈dom⁡(σ)\bm{x}\in\mathrm{dom}(\sigma) is of length at most ℓ\ell. A structured graph is a pair 𝑮=(G,σ)\bm{G}=(G,\sigma), where GG is a graph and σ\sigma is a structure map on GG.

Examples 3.6.
  1. (i)

    A labeled graph (G,f)(G,f) in the sense of Definition 1.35 can be viewed as a structured graph by identifying V⁡(G)V(G) with V​(G)1V(G)^{1} in the obvious way.

  2. (ii)

    A directed graph GG can be viewed as a structured graph by encoding the directions of the arcs of GG using the function σ:V​(G)2→2\sigma\colon V(G)^{2}\to 2 that sends a pair (u,v)(u,v) to 11 if and only if there is an arc from uu to vv in GG.

  3. (iii)

    An ordered graph is a pair (G,≼)(G,\preccurlyeq), where GG is a graph and ≼\preccurlyeq is a linear order on V⁡(G)V(G). These objects are of interest in extremal combinatorics [Tar19]. An ordered graph can be represented by a structured graph using the map σ:V​(G)2→2\sigma\colon V(G)^{2}\to 2, where σ⁡(u,v)=1\sigma(u,v)=1 if and only if u≼vu\preccurlyeq v.

A structured graph 𝑮=(G,σ)\bm{G}=(G,\sigma) is Borel if GG is a Borel graph and σ\sigma is a Borel function (that is, σ−1​(i)\sigma^{-1}(i) is a Borel subset of V​(G)<∞V(G)^{<\infty} for all i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}).

We naturally extend standard graph-theoretic notation and terminology to structured graphs. For example, given a structured graph 𝑮=(G,σ)\bm{G}=(G,\sigma), we write V⁡(𝑮)≔V⁡(G)V(\bm{G})\coloneqq V(G) and E⁡(𝑮)≔E⁡(G)E(\bm{G})\coloneqq E(G). Similarly, given v∈V⁡(𝑮)v\in V(\bm{G}) and R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}, we let

B𝑮​(v,R)≔BG​(v,R)⊆V⁡(𝑮).B_{\bm{G}}(v,R)\,\coloneqq\,B_{G}(v,R)\,\subseteq\,V(\bm{G}).

For a subset U⊆V⁡(𝑮)U\subseteq V(\bm{G}), the subgraph of 𝑮\bm{G} induced by UU is the structured graph 𝑮⁡[U]\bm{G}[U] given by

𝑮⁡[U]≔(G⁡[U],σ|U<∞).\bm{G}[U]\,\coloneqq\,\big(G[U],{{\sigma}|_{U^{<\infty}}}\big).

Isomorphisms between structured graphs are required to preserve the values of the structure maps. We also let 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(𝑮)≔𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)\mathsf{asi}(\bm{G})\coloneqq\mathsf{asi}(G).

With this we can define labelings of structured graphs, rooted (labeled) structured graphs, LCL problems and their solutions, 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms, and deterministic and randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity of LCL problems on structured graphs by simply repeating Definitions 1.35, 1.37, 1.38, and 1.39 with every occurrence of the word “graph” replaced by “structured graph.” Theorems 1.40 and 1.41 remain true in this more general context [Ber23, Theorems 2.10 and 2.14], and the same is true for our Theorem 1.42:

In fact, we can strengthen Theorem 3.7 by avoiding the asymptotic notation o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n). Let 𝔾\mathbb{G} be a class of finite structured graphs and let RR, n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}. A structured graph 𝑮\bm{G} is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝔾\mathbb{G} if for all v∈V⁡(𝑮)v\in V(\bm{G}), there is exist an nn-vertex structured graph 𝑯∈𝔾\bm{H}\in\mathbb{G} and u∈V⁡(𝑯)u\in V(\bm{H}) such that

(𝑮⁡[B𝑮​(v,R)],v)≅(𝑯⁡[B𝑯​(u,R)],u)\big(\bm{G}[B_{\bm{G}}(v,R)],\,v\big)\,\cong\,\big(\bm{H}[B_{\bm{H}}(u,R)],\,u\big)

as rooted structured graphs.

The bound on |B𝑮​(v,2​R∗)||B_{\bm{G}}(v,2R^{\ast})| in Theorem 3.8 depends on the exact value of 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(𝑮)\mathsf{asi}(\bm{G}). We also prove an analogous statement with a uniform bound for all 𝑮\bm{G} with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(𝑮)<∞\mathsf{asi}(\bm{G})<\infty:

The chain of implications between our main results is as follows:

Theorem 1.29⇒(A)Theorem 3.8⇒(B)Theorem 3.7⇒(C)Theorem 1.31⇒(D)Theorem 3.9.\text{Theorem\penalty\ \ref{theo:main_easy_asi}}\,\xRightarrow{\text{{(}{A}{)}}}\,\text{Theorem\penalty\ \ref{theo:LOCAL_main}}\,\xRightarrow{\text{{(}{B}{)}}}\,\text{Theorem\penalty\ \ref{theo:rand_LOCAL_to_asi_structured}}\,\xRightarrow{\text{{(}{C}{)}}}\,\text{Theorem\penalty\ \ref{theo:main_speedup}}\,\xRightarrow{\text{{(}{D}{)}}}\,\text{Theorem\penalty\ \ref{theo:LOCAL_main_speedup}}.

Theorem 1.29 has been verified in §3.1, so now we are left with proving the four implications in the above diagram. In this subsection, we shall establish implications (A), (B), and (D). The only remaining implication, (C), will be proved in §3.3.

We start with implication (B), which is proved by a straightforward computation.

Proof of implication (B): Theorem 3.8 ⟹\Longrightarrow Theorem 3.7.

This argument is essentially present in [Ber23] (immediately following [Ber23, Theorem 2.10]). Assume that Theorem 3.8 holds and let Π=(R,𝒫)\Pi=(R,\mathcal{P}), 𝔾\mathbb{G}, and 𝑮\bm{G} be as in Theorem 3.7. If 𝑮\bm{G} is finite, then 𝑮\bm{G} itself is in 𝔾\mathbb{G}, and so it has an (automatically Borel) Π\Pi-coloring. Thus, we may assume that 𝑮\bm{G} is infinite. We now claim that the conditions of Theorem 3.8 are satisfied for all large enough n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, and thus 𝑮\bm{G} has a Borel Π\Pi-coloring, as desired.

Let the maximum degree of 𝑮\bm{G} be Δ\Delta and let s≔𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(𝑮)s\coloneqq\mathsf{asi}(\bm{G}). Let

t⁡(n)≔𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝔾​(n)andR∗​(n)≔t⁡(n)+R.t(n)\,\coloneqq\,\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathbb{G}}(n)\qquad\text{and}\qquad R^{\ast}(n)\,\coloneqq\,t(n)+R.

Consider any vertex v∈V⁡(𝑮)v\in V(\bm{G}) and let B≔B𝑮​(v,R∗​(n))B\coloneqq B_{\bm{G}}(v,R^{\ast}(n)). If n⩾|B|n\geqslant|B|, then we can extend BB to an nn-element set U⊇BU\supseteq B of vertices and observe that the R∗​(n)R^{\ast}(n)-balls around vv in 𝑮\bm{G} and 𝑮⁡[U]\bm{G}[U] are the same. Since every finite induced subgraph of 𝑮\bm{G} is in 𝔾\mathbb{G}, it follows that GG is (R∗​(n),n)(R^{\ast}(n),n)-locally in 𝔾\mathbb{G} provided that nn is at least as large as the size of every R∗​(n)R^{\ast}(n)-ball in 𝑮\bm{G}.

Since t⁡(n)=o⁡(log⁡n)t(n)=o(\log n) and hence Δt⁡(n)=no⁡(1)\Delta^{t(n)}=n^{o(1)}, the following chain of inequalities holds for all sufficiently large n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}:

(3.7) 1+ΔR∗​(n)⩽ 1+Δ2​R∗​(n)= 1+Δ2​t​(n)+2​R⩽n1/(s+1)/e⩽n.1+\Delta^{R^{*}(n)}\,\leqslant\,1+\Delta^{2R^{*}(n)}\,=\,1+\Delta^{2t(n)+2R}\,\leqslant\,n^{1/(s+1)}/e\,\leqslant\,n.

As every rr-ball in 𝑮\bm{G} contains at most 1+Δr1+\Delta^{r} vertices, any nn satisfying the bounds in (3.7) fulfills all the requirements of Theorem 3.8, and we are done. ∎

3.3.  From LOCAL\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms to the LLL

In this section we verify the only remaining implication from the diagram in §3.2, namely (C): Theorem 3.7 ⟹\Longrightarrow Theorem 1.31. Our argument follows the strategy outlined in [Ber23, §5.D]. The key point is that there exist efficient randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms that solve CSPs satisfying a polynomial LLL criterion, and combining such an algorithm with Theorem 3.7 yields Borel solutions to such CSPs when the associated graph has finite asymptotic separation index.

To make the above idea precise, we need to be able to encode a given CSP as an LCL problem on an auxiliary structured graph. There are several natural ways of doing so; here we follow the approach described in [Ber23, §5.D].

Definition 3.11 (Graph-CSPs).

A graph-CSP with range q∈ℕ+q\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} is a pair (G,ℬ)(G,\mathscr{B}), where GG is a graph and ℬ:V(G)→?q\mathscr{B}\colon V(G)\to^{?}q is a bounded CSP such that 𝖽⁡(ℬ)<∞\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})<\infty and GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} is a subgraph of GG.

A graph-CSP (G,ℬ)(G,\mathscr{B}) can be viewed as a structured graph in the following way. For each tuple of vertices 𝒗=(v0,…,vk−1)∈V​(G)<∞\bm{v}=(v_{0},\ldots,v_{k-1})\in V(G)^{<\infty}, the structure map σ\sigma will contain the information about the constraints B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} such that dom⁡(B)={v0,…,vk−1}\mathrm{dom}(B)=\{v_{0},\ldots,v_{k-1}\}. Formally, let (V⁡(G))<∞(V(G))^{<\infty} be the set of all finite tuples of distinct vertices and for each 𝒗=(v0,…,vk−1)∈(V⁡(G))<∞\bm{v}=(v_{0},\ldots,v_{k-1})\in(V(G))^{<\infty}, define

ℬ𝒗≔{B∈ℬ:dom⁡(B)={v0,…,vk−1}}.\mathscr{B}_{\bm{v}}\,\coloneqq\,\{B\in\mathscr{B}\,:\,\mathrm{dom}(B)=\{v_{0},\ldots,v_{k-1}\}\}.

The domain of σ\sigma is the set of all 𝒗∈(V⁡(G))<∞\bm{v}\in(V(G))^{<\infty} with ℬ𝒗≠∅\mathscr{B}_{\bm{v}}\neq\varnothing. Note that since ℬ\mathscr{B} is bounded, σ\sigma is defined on tuples of bounded length. For 𝒗=(v0,…,vk−1)∈dom⁡(σ)\bm{v}=(v_{0},\ldots,v_{k-1})\in\mathrm{dom}(\sigma), let ι𝒗:{v0,…,vk−1}→k\iota_{\bm{v}}\colon\{v_{0},\ldots,v_{k-1}\}\to k be the bijection given by ι𝒗​(xi)≔i\iota_{\bm{v}}(x_{i})\coloneqq i, and for each B∈ℬ𝒗B\in\mathscr{B}_{\bm{v}}, define

B𝒗∗≔{φ:k→q:φ∘ι𝒗∈B}.B_{\bm{v}}^{\ast}\,\coloneqq\,\{\varphi\colon k\to q\,:\,\varphi\circ\iota_{\bm{v}}\in B\}.

Note that the mapping B𝒗∗→B:φ↦φ∘ι𝒗B^{\ast}_{\bm{v}}\to B\colon\varphi\mapsto\varphi\circ\iota_{\bm{v}} is a bijection. Now let the type of 𝒗\bm{v} be

𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾⁡(𝒗)≔{B𝒗∗:B∈ℬ𝒗}.\mathsf{type}(\bm{v})\,\coloneqq\,\{B^{\ast}_{\bm{v}}\,:\,B\in\mathscr{B}_{\bm{v}}\}.

Observe that the set 𝖳𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Types} of all possible types of tuples in dom⁡(σ)\mathrm{dom}(\sigma) is countable (indeed, it is a subset of [[[ℕ⇢ℕ]<∞]<∞]<∞{[{{{[{{{[{{{\mathbb{N}}}\dashrightarrow{{\mathbb{N}}}}]^{{<\infty}}}}}]^{{<\infty}}}}}]^{{<\infty}}}), so we can fix an arbitrary injection 𝖼𝗈𝖽𝖾:𝖳𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗌→ℕ\mathsf{code}\colon\mathsf{Types}\to{\mathbb{N}} and let

σ⁡(𝒗)≔𝖼𝗈𝖽𝖾⁡(𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾⁡(𝒗)).\sigma(\bm{v})\,\coloneqq\,\mathsf{code}(\mathsf{type}(\bm{v})).

The pair (G,σ)(G,\sigma) now represents exactly the same information as (G,ℬ)(G,\mathscr{B}), and since σ\sigma is defined on tuples of bounded length, (G,σ)(G,\sigma) is a structured graph (as in Definition 3.5). Moreover, it is routine to check that if GG is a Borel graph and ℬ\mathscr{B} is a Borel CSP, then σ\sigma is a Borel function, and thus (G,σ)(G,\sigma) is a Borel structured graph.

Let (G,ℬ)(G,\mathscr{B}) be a graph-CSP. The requirement that GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} is a subgraph of GG means that the 11-ball around every vertex of GG includes the domains of all constraints that involve that vertex. That is, the problem of solving a graph-CSP is an LCL problem of radius 11, which we denote by ΠCSP,q\Pi_{\mathrm{CSP},q} (here q∈ℕ+q\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} is the range of ℬ\mathscr{B}). Given parameters qq, kk, pp, and dd, let ℂ​𝕊​ℙ​(q,k,p,d)\mathbb{CSP}(q,k,p,d) be the class of all finite graph-CSPs (G,ℬ)(G,\mathscr{B}) (viewed as structured graphs) such that:

  • —

    the range of ℬ\mathscr{B} is qq;

  • —

    supB∈ℬ|dom⁡(B)|⩽k\sup_{B\in\mathscr{B}}|\mathrm{dom}(B)|\leqslant k;

  • —

    𝗉⁡(ℬ)⩽p\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant p and 𝖽⁡(ℬ)⩽d\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant d.

After these technical preliminaries, we can rigorously formulate a result regarding 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms for the LLL that we shall use:

Theorem 3.12 (Ghaffari–Harris–Kuhn [GHK18]).

If qq, kk, pp, and dd satisfy p​(d+1)8⩽2−15p(d+1)^{8}\leqslant 2^{-15}, then

𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽ΠCSP,q,ℂ​𝕊​ℙ​(q,k,p,d)​(n)=exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡log⁡n))=o⁡(log⁡n).\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi_{\mathrm{CSP},q},\,\mathbb{CSP}(q,k,p,d)}(n)\,=\,\exp(O(\sqrt{\log\log n}))\,=\,o(\log n).

The first o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n)-time randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm for the LLL with a polynomial criterion is due to Fischer and Ghaffari [FG17]. We are using the Ghaffari–Harris–Kuhn version instead because it improves the criterion from 𝗉​(𝖽+1)32⩽e−32\mathsf{p}(\mathsf{d}+1)^{32}\leqslant e^{-32} to 𝗉​(𝖽+1)8⩽2−15\mathsf{p}(\mathsf{d}+1)^{8}\leqslant 2^{-15}. In subsequent work, considerable effort has been put into making the running time of the algorithm even lower [RG20, Dav23]. On the other hand, we are not aware of any improvements to the required bound on 𝗉\mathsf{p} as a function of 𝖽\mathsf{d}, and it remains an open problem whether the exponent 88 can be reduced, ideally all the way down to 11.

With Theorem 3.12 in hand, we are ready to deduce Theorem 1.31 from Theorem 3.7:

Proof of implication (C): Theorem 3.7 ⟹\Longrightarrow Theorem 1.31.

Let ℬ:X→?q\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}q be a bounded Borel CSP on a standard Borel space XX such that 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G_{\mathscr{B}})<\infty and

𝗉⁡(ℬ)​(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)8⩽ 2−15.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\,(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)^{8}\,\leqslant\,2^{-15}.

Let p≔𝗉⁡(ℬ)p\coloneqq\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}), d≔𝖽⁡(ℬ)d\coloneqq\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}), and k≔supB∈ℬ|dom⁡(B)|k\coloneqq\sup_{B\in\mathscr{B}}|\mathrm{dom}(B)|, and let Π≔ΠCSP,q\Pi\coloneqq\Pi_{\mathrm{CSP},q} and 𝔾≔ℂ​𝕊​ℙ​(q,k,p,d)\mathbb{G}\coloneqq\mathbb{CSP}(q,k,p,d). By the usual LLL, the structured graphs in 𝔾\mathbb{G} are Π\Pi-colorable. Furthermore, by Theorem 3.12, we have 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝔾​(n)=o⁡(log⁡n)\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathbb{G}}(n)=o(\log n). Consider the graph-CSP 𝑮≔(Gℬ,ℬ)\bm{G}\coloneqq(G_{\mathscr{B}},\mathscr{B}), viewed as a Borel structured graph. The maximum degree of 𝑮\bm{G} is bounded above by k​dkd, and all finite induced subgraphs of 𝑮\bm{G} are in 𝔾\mathbb{G} (taking an induced subgraph corresponds to passing to a subset of the vertices and only retaining the constraints whose domains are contained in that subset). Since 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(𝑮)<∞\mathsf{asi}(\bm{G})<\infty by assumption, we conclude that 𝑮\bm{G} has a Borel Π\Pi-coloring—i.e., ℬ\mathscr{B} has a Borel solution—by Theorem 3.7. ∎

4.  Applications

4.1.  Coloring graphs without short cycles

Here we present the derivation of Theorem 1.18 from our main results. For Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}, let 𝕋​r​𝔽​reeΔ\mathbb{T}\mathrm{r}\mathbb{F}\mathrm{ree}_{\Delta} be the class of all triangle-free finite graphs of maximum degree at most Δ\Delta. Given ε>0\varepsilon>0 and Δ⩾2\Delta\geqslant 2, let

q⁡(Δ,ε)≔⌊(4+ε)​Δlog⁡Δ⌋.q(\Delta,\varepsilon)\,\coloneqq\,\left\lfloor(4+\varepsilon)\frac{\Delta}{\log\Delta}\right\rfloor.

Let Πq\Pi_{q} denote the LCL problem that encodes proper qq-coloring of graphs (see Example 1.36). Chung, Pettie, and Su [CPS17, Theorem 9] showed that for each ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exist CC, δ\delta, Δ0>0\Delta_{0}>0 (depending on ε\varepsilon) such that for every Δ⩾Δ0\Delta\geqslant\Delta_{0}, we have

(4.1) 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Πq⁡(Δ,ε),𝕋​r​𝔽​reeΔ​(n)⩽C​Δ−δ​log⁡n.\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi_{q(\Delta,\varepsilon)},\,\mathbb{T}\mathrm{r}\mathbb{F}\mathrm{ree}_{\Delta}}(n)\,\leqslant\,C\Delta^{-\delta}\log n.

Although this bound is not strong enough to invoke Theorem 1.42 (it is of order O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rather than o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n)), it is still sufficient for a direct application of Theorem 3.9.**** ** Actually, the running time of the Chung–Pettie–Su algorithm can be improved to o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n) via generic “speed-up” theorems in distributed computing, namely by combining a result of Chang and Pettie [CP19, Theorem 6] with an o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n)-time randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm for the LLL such as Theorem 3.12. That being said, the bound (4.1) suffices for our purposes. Indeed, the same analysis as in the proof of the implication Theorem 3.8 ⟹\Longrightarrow Theorem 3.7 on page 3.2 reduces the problem to showing that for all sufficiently large n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}},

1+Δ2​C​Δ−δ​log⁡n+2⩽14​n1/8.1+\Delta^{2C\Delta^{-\delta}\log n+2}\,\leqslant\,\frac{1}{4}n^{1/8}.

This is indeed the case as long as Δ\Delta is large enough as a function of ε\varepsilon, since

Δ2​C​Δ−δ​log⁡n=n2​C​Δ−δ​log⁡Δ,\Delta^{2C\Delta^{-\delta}\log n}\,=\,n^{2C\Delta^{-\delta}\log\Delta},

and 2​C​Δ−δ​log⁡Δ<1/82C\Delta^{-\delta}\log\Delta<1/8 for sufficiently large Δ\Delta. This establishes the part of Theorem 1.18 regarding triangle-free graphs. The part of Theorem 1.18 concerning graphs without 33- and 44-cycles is proved in exactly the same way, but with [CPS17, Theorem 9] replaced by the randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm of Chung, Pettie, and Su for ⌊(1+ε)​Δ/log⁡Δ⌋\lfloor(1+\varepsilon)\Delta/\log\Delta\rfloor-coloring graphs without cycles of length at most 44 (see the remark in [CPS17] after [CPS17, Theorem 9]).

4.2.  Edge-colorings with Δ+O~​(Δ)\Delta+\tilde{O}(\sqrt{\Delta}) colors

In this subsection, we prove Theorem 1.49. We begin by explaining how to frame proper edge-coloring as an LCL problem. The obvious approach is to view proper qq-edge-coloring of a graph GG as a proper qq-coloring of the line graph L⁡(G)L(G) and use the LCL problem defined in Example 1.36. The drawback of this strategy is that 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms for edge-coloring typically reference both edges and vertices of GG, and the information about the vertices of GG is apparently lost when working on L⁡(G)L(G). However, this issue can be easily rectified by incorporating both the vertices and the edges of GG into an auxiliary structure. For example, we can use the following construction, suggested in [Cha20, 5]. Let GG be a graph. Define a new graph G′G^{\prime} with vertex set V⁡(G′)≔V⁡(G)⊔E⁡(G)V(G^{\prime})\coloneqq V(G)\sqcup E(G) and edge set E(G′)≔{{v,e}:v∈V(G),e∈E(G),v∈e}E(G^{\prime})\coloneqq\{\{v,e\}\,:\,v\in V(G),\,e\in E(G),\,v\in e\}. For all v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) and e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G), let σ⁡(v)≔0\sigma(v)\coloneqq 0 and σ⁡(e)≔1\sigma(e)\coloneqq 1. This defines a function σ:V⁡(G′)→2\sigma\colon V(G^{\prime})\to 2 and yields a structured graph 𝑮′≔(G′,σ)\bm{G^{\prime}}\coloneqq(G^{\prime},\sigma), which contains information about the vertices and edges of GG, distinguished from each other via the map σ\sigma. Proper qq-edge-coloring of GG can be encoded as an LCL problem on 𝑮′\bm{G^{\prime}} of radius 22, which requires every vertex xx of 𝑮′\bm{G^{\prime}} with σ⁡(x)=1\sigma(x)=1 to receive a label in qq that is distinct from the labels of the vertices joined to xx by paths of length 22.

Fix Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}} and let q≔⌊Δ+Δ​log3​Δ⌋q\coloneqq\lfloor\Delta+\sqrt{\Delta}\log^{3}\Delta\rfloor. Combining a result of Chang, He, Li, Pettie, and Uitto [Cha+19, Theorem 4] with a randomized LLL algorithm due to Fischer and Ghaffari [FG17] (or with Theorem 3.12), we see that the proper qq-edge-coloring problem can be solved on nn-vertex graphs of maximum degree Δ\Delta by a randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm with running time o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n), assuming Δ\Delta is sufficiently large. By Theorem 3.9, it follows that every Borel graph GG with finite asymptotic separation index and of maximum degree Δ\Delta has a Borel proper qq-edge-coloring, as desired.

For further discussion of the state of the art in distributed edge-coloring, see [Dav23].

4.3.  Borel independent complete sections

Here we prove Theorem 1.53, restated below for ease of reference.

Theorem 1.53.

Let HH be a Borel graph with 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(H)<∞\mathsf{asi}(H)<\infty and let G1G_{1}, G2G_{2} be two spanning Borel subgraphs of HH. Suppose that the maximum degree of G1G_{1} is at most Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}, where Δ⩾2\Delta\geqslant 2. If every component of G2G_{2} contains at least 225​Δ​log⁡Δ2^{25}\,\Delta\log\Delta vertices, then there is a Borel G1G_{1}-independent complete section for G2G_{2}.

Proof of Theorem 4.3.

For brevity, let V≔V⁡(H)V\coloneqq V(H). Let k≔⌈225​Δ​log⁡Δ⌉k\coloneqq\lceil 2^{25}\Delta\log\Delta\rceil, so every component of G2G_{2} has at least kk vertices. In fact, we may assume that every component of G2G_{2} contains exactly kk vertices. Indeed, let ℛ⊆[V]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{V}}]^{{<\infty}}} be the family of all finite sets RR such that:

  • —

    |R|=k|R|=k, and

  • —

    the graph G2​[R]G_{2}[R] is connected.

By [KM04, Lemma 7.3], there exists a Borel set ℛ′⊆ℛ\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{R} such that the members of ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} are pairwise disjoint and every set in ℛ\mathcal{R} intersects some member of ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime}. It follows that the vertex set of every connected component of G2G_{2} includes at least one member of ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} as a subset. Now define U≔⋃ℛ′U\coloneqq\bigcup\mathcal{R}^{\prime}, H′≔H⁡[U]H^{\prime}\coloneqq H[U], G1′≔G1​[U]G_{1}^{\prime}\coloneqq G_{1}[U], and let G2′G_{2}^{\prime} be the spanning subgraph of G2​[U]G_{2}[U] obtained by only retaining the edges of the graphs G2​[R]G_{2}[R] with R∈ℛ′R\in\mathcal{R}^{\prime} (in other words, G2′G_{2}^{\prime} is the graph whose connected components are precisely the graphs G2​[R]G_{2}[R] with R∈ℛ′R\in\mathcal{R}^{\prime}). Then H′H^{\prime}, G1′G_{1}^{\prime}, and G2′G_{2}^{\prime} are Borel graphs satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 4.3. Furthermore, by construction, every component of G2′G_{2}^{\prime} contains exactly kk vertices. Suppose we can find a Borel G1′G_{1}^{\prime}-independent complete section SS for G2′G_{2}^{\prime}. Then SS is G1G_{1}-independent (because G1′G_{1}^{\prime} is an induced subgraph of G1G_{1}) and a complete section for G2G_{2} (because every component of G2G_{2} includes a component of G2′G_{2}^{\prime}). Therefore, proving the theorem under the assumption that every component of G2G_{2} contains exactly kk vertices implies the theorem in general.

Let G≔G1G\coloneqq G_{1} and ℱ≔{V⁡(C):C is a connected component of G2}\mathcal{F}\coloneqq\{V(C)\,:\,\text{$C$ is a connected component of $G_{2}$}\}. Then ℱ\mathcal{F} is a Borel subset of [V]k[V]^{k}, and our goal is to find a Borel GG-independent complete section for ℱ\mathcal{F}. Without loss of generality, we may assume that each set F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} is GG-independent. To see this, let G′G^{\prime} be the spanning subgraph of GG in which two vertices are adjacent if and only if they are adjacent in GG and do not belong to the same set in ℱ\mathcal{F} (so each set F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} is G′G^{\prime}-independent by construction). Suppose we can find a Borel G′G^{\prime}-independent complete section SS for ℱ\mathcal{F}. Using the Luzin–Novikov theorem (Theorem 2.2), we can choose, for each F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}, a single vertex vF∈S∩Fv_{F}\in S\cap F so that the mapping ℱ→S:F↦vF\mathcal{F}\to S\colon F\mapsto v_{F} is Borel. Then S′≔{vF:F∈ℱ}S^{\prime}\coloneqq\{v_{F}\,:\,F\in\mathcal{F}\} is a Borel subset of SS that meets every set in ℱ\mathcal{F} in exactly one vertex. It follows that S′S^{\prime} is GG-independent, so we have found a Borel GG-independent complete section for ℱ\mathcal{F}.

With these preparations, we may start the main part of the proof. Given a Δ\Delta-coloring f:V→Δf\colon V\to\Delta, we define a set Sf⊆VS_{f}\subseteq V by

Sf≔{v∈V:f⁡(v)=0​ and ​f​(u)≠0​ for all ​u​v∈E⁡(G)}.S_{f}\,\coloneqq\,\{v\in V\,:\,f(v)=0\text{ and }f(u)\neq 0\text{ for all }uv\in E(G)\}.

By construction, SfS_{f} is a GG-independent set, and if ff is a Borel function, then SfS_{f} is Borel. Our aim is to find a Borel function f:V→Δf\colon V\to\Delta such that SfS_{f} meets every set in ℱ\mathcal{F}.

The membership of a vertex vv in SfS_{f} is determined by the values of ff at vv and the neighbors of vv. Thus, whether SfS_{f} meets a set F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} only depends on the restriction of ff to BG​(F,1)B_{G}(F,1), i.e., the set of all vertices that are in FF or have a GG-neighbor in FF. Hence, we can define a (V,Δ)(V,\Delta)-constraint BFB_{F} with domain BG​(F,1)B_{G}(F,1) such that f:V→Δf\colon V\to\Delta satisfies BFB_{F} if and only if SfS_{f} meets FF. Explicitly,

BF≔{φ:BG(F,1)→Δ:for all v∈F, φ⁡(v)≠0 or φ⁡(u)=0 for some u​v∈E⁡(G)}.B_{F}\,\coloneqq\,\big\{\varphi\colon B_{G}(F,1)\to\Delta\ :\ \text{for all $v\in F$, $\varphi(v)\neq 0$ or $\varphi(u)=0$ for some $uv\in E(G)$}\big\}.

Let ℬ≔{BF:F∈ℱ}\mathscr{B}\coloneqq\{B_{F}\,:\,F\in\mathcal{F}\}. This is a bounded Borel CSP such that if f:V→Δf\colon V\to\Delta is a solution to ℬ\mathscr{B}, then SfS_{f} is a Borel GG-independent complete section for ℱ\mathcal{F}. It remains to argue that ℬ\mathscr{B} has a Borel solution, to which end we shall employ Theorem 1.31.

To begin with, we observe that 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G_{\mathscr{B}})<\infty. Indeed, if uu and vv are neighbors in GℬG_{\mathscr{B}}, then there is some F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} such that uu, v∈BG​(F,1)v\in B_{G}(F,1). Since H⁡[F]H[F] is a connected graph with at most kk vertices, it follows that uu and vv are joined by a path of at most k+1k+1 edges in HH. Thus, GℬG_{\mathscr{B}} is a subgraph of Hk+1H^{k+1}, and hence 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(Gℬ)⩽𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(H)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G_{\mathscr{B}})\leqslant\mathsf{asi}(H)<\infty. We will not use the graph HH again, so all the references to neighbors, adjacency, edges, etc. in the sequel are in relation to the graph GG.

Next we need to bound the parameters 𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}) and 𝗉⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}). We start with 𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}), which is the easier one. Take F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} and suppose that F′∈ℱ∖{F}F^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}\setminus\{F\} satisfies BG​(F′,1)∩BG​(F,1)≠∅B_{G}(F^{\prime},1)\cap B_{G}(F,1)\neq\varnothing. Consider any vertex v∈BG​(F,1)∩BG​(F′,1)v\in B_{G}(F,1)\cap B_{G}(F^{\prime},1). Since v∈BG​(F,1)v\in B_{G}(F,1), there are at most k+Δ​kk+\Delta k choices for vv. As v∈BG​(F′,1)v\in B_{G}(F^{\prime},1), either vv itself or a neighbor of vv is in F′F^{\prime}. Since the sets in ℱ\mathcal{F} are disjoint, it follows that, given vv, there are at most 1+Δ1+\Delta choices for F′F^{\prime}. In total, for fixed FF, there are at most (k+Δ​k)​(1+Δ)−1(k+\Delta k)(1+\Delta)-1 options for F′F^{\prime} (we are subtracting 11 since FF itself should not be counted), so

𝖽⁡(ℬ)⩽(k+Δ​k)​(1+Δ)−1⩽ 4​Δ2​k−1⩽ 227​Δ5−1.\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})\,\leqslant\,(k+\Delta k)(1+\Delta)-1\,\leqslant\,4\Delta^{2}k-1\,\leqslant\,2^{27}\Delta^{5}-1.

Now we turn our attention to 𝗉⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}). Consider any set F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}. We need to bound ℙ⁡[BF]\mathbb{P}[B_{F}], i.e., the probability that a uniformly random Δ\Delta-coloring φ:BG​(F,1)→Δ\varphi\colon B_{G}(F,1)\to\Delta belongs to the set BFB_{F}. Let NN be the set of all neighbors of the vertices in FF, and let ψ:N→Δ\psi\colon N\to\Delta and ξ:F→Δ\xi\colon F\to\Delta be the restrictions of φ\varphi to NN and FF respectively. By our assumption, the set FF is GG-independent, so, BG​(F,1)=F⊔NB_{G}(F,1)=F\sqcup N, which means that ψ\psi and ξ\xi are chosen independently and uniformly at random from the sets of all Δ\Delta-colorings of NN and FF respectively. Let

(4.3) ℙ[BF]=ℙ[ξ(v)≠0 for all v∈F∗].\mathbb{P}[B_{F}]\,=\,\mathbb{P}[\xi(v)\neq 0\text{ for all }v\in F^{\ast}].

The key observation is that |F∗||F^{\ast}| is unlikely to be too small:

Claim 4.1.

ℙ[|F∗|<k/8]⩽ 4Δ−500.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[|F^{\ast}|<k/8]\,\leqslant\,4\Delta^{-500}.

Proof.

Observe that, since (1−1/x)x⩾(1−1/2)2=1/4(1-1/x)^{x}\geqslant(1-1/2)^{2}=1/4 for all x⩾2x\geqslant 2, we have

𝔼⁡[|F∗|]⩾|F|​(1−1Δ)Δ⩾k4.\mathbb{E}[|F^{\ast}|]\,\geqslant\,|F|\left(1-\frac{1}{\Delta}\right)^{\Delta}\,\geqslant\,\frac{k}{4}.

To this end, we shall apply a concentration of measure result that is often used in probabilistic combinatorics and is a consequence of Talagrand’s isoperimetric inequality [Tal95]. There are several variants of this inequality in the literature [MR14, BJ18, KP20], and designing new and improved versions of it is an active area of research. We shall use a (simplified form of) the recent formulation due to Delcourt and Postle [DP22]. Given two finite strings x=(x1,…,xn){x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) and y=(y1,…,yn){y}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}), and a vector c=(c1,…,cn)∈ℝn{c}=(c_{1},\ldots,c_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we let

𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍c(x,y)≔∑i:xi≠yi|ci|.\mathsf{dist}_{{c}}({x},{y})\,\coloneqq\,\sum_{i\,:\,x_{i}\neq y_{i}}|c_{i}|.
Theorem 4.2 (Talagrand’s inequality; Delcourt–Postle [DP22, Theorem 4.4]).

Let (Ω1,μ1)(\Omega_{1},\mu_{1}), …, (Ωn,μn)(\Omega_{n},\mu_{n}) be discrete probability spaces and let (Ω,μ)≔∏i=1n(Ωi,μi)(\Omega,\mu)\coloneqq\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\Omega_{i},\mu_{i}) be their product space. Then for any t>96​r​d​𝔼​[X]+128​r​dt>96\sqrt{rd\mathbb{E}[X]}+128rd,

ℙ[|X−𝔼[X]|>t]⩽ 4exp(−t28​r​d​(4​𝔼​[X]+t)).\mathbb{P}\left[|X-\mathbb{E}[X]|>t\right]\,\leqslant\,4\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{8rd(4\mathbb{E}[X]+t)}\right).

To apply this in our setting, we view ψ:N→Δ\psi\colon N\to\Delta as a point in the product of |N||N| copies of the space (Δ,ν)(\Delta,\nu), where ν\nu is the uniform probability measure on the set Δ={0,1,…,Δ−1}\Delta=\{0,1,\ldots,\Delta-1\}. Let

c⁡(u)≔|{v∈F∖F∗​(ψ):u=uv}|.c(u)\,\coloneqq\,|\{v\in F\setminus F^{\ast}(\psi)\,:\,u=u_{v}\}|.

Now take any ψ′:N→Δ\psi^{\prime}\colon N\to\Delta and note that if v∈F∗​(ψ′)∖F∗​(ψ)v\in F^{\ast}(\psi^{\prime})\setminus F^{\ast}(\psi), then ψ′​(uv)≠0\psi^{\prime}(u_{v})\neq 0, so

X(ψ′)⩾X(ψ)−|F∗(ψ′)∖F∗(ψ)|⩾X(ψ)−∑u:ψ′​(u)≠0c(u)=X(ψ′)−𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍c(ψ,ψ′),X(\psi^{\prime})\,\geqslant\,X(\psi)-|F^{\ast}(\psi^{\prime})\setminus F^{\ast}(\psi)|\,\geqslant\,X(\psi)-\sum_{u\,:\,\psi^{\prime}(u)\neq 0}c(u)\,=\,X(\psi^{\prime})-\mathsf{dist}_{c}(\psi,\psi^{\prime}),

as desired. Since 𝔼⁡[X]⩽k\mathbb{E}[X]\leqslant k and k/8>96​Δ​k+128​Δk/8>96\sqrt{\Delta k}+128\Delta, we may now apply Theorem 4.2 with r=1r=1, d=Δd=\Delta, and t=k/8t=k/8 to conclude that

ℙ[|F∗|<𝔼[|F∗|]−k/8]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\big[|F^{\ast}|<\mathbb{E}[|F^{\ast}|]-k/8\big]\, =ℙ[X−𝔼[X]>k/8]\displaystyle=\,\mathbb{P}[X-\mathbb{E}[X]>k/8]
⩽ 4​exp⁡(−k2/648​Δ​(4​k+k/8))= 4​exp⁡(−k2112​Δ)⩽ 4​Δ−500,\displaystyle\leqslant\,4\exp\left(-\frac{k^{2}/64}{8\Delta(4k+k/8)}\right)\,=\,4\exp\left(-\frac{k}{2112\Delta}\right)\,\leqslant\,4\Delta^{-500},

where the last inequality uses the bound k⩾225​Δ​log⁡Δk\geqslant 2^{25}\,\Delta\log\Delta. ∎

Note that the definition of the set F∗F^{\ast} depends on ψ\psi but not on ξ\xi. Since the functions ψ:N→Δ\psi\colon N\to\Delta and ξ:F→Δ\xi\colon F\to\Delta are chosen independently, conditioned on the choice of ψ\psi, we can write

ℙ⁡[ξ⁡(v)≠0​ for all ​v∈F∗|ψ]=(1−1Δ)|F∗|.\mathbb{P}[\xi(v)\neq 0\text{ for all }v\in F^{\ast}\,|\,\psi]\,=\,\left(1-\frac{1}{\Delta}\right)^{|F^{\ast}|}.

ℙ[ξ(v)≠0 for all v∈F∗]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\xi(v)\neq 0\text{ for all }v\in F^{\ast}]\, ⩽ 4​Δ−500+(1−1Δ)k/8\displaystyle\leqslant\,4\Delta^{-500}\,+\,\left(1-\frac{1}{\Delta}\right)^{k/8}
(since ​1−x⩽e−x​ for all ​x∈ℝ)\displaystyle\big(\text{since }1-x\leqslant e^{-x}\text{ for all }x\in\mathbb{R}\big)\qquad\qquad ⩽ 4​Δ−500+exp⁡(−k8​Δ)⩽ 5​Δ−500,\displaystyle\leqslant\,4\Delta^{-500}\,+\,\exp\left(-\frac{k}{8\Delta}\right)\,\leqslant\,5\Delta^{-500},

where the last inequality uses the bound k⩾225​Δ​log⁡Δk\geqslant 2^{25}\Delta\log\Delta. Remembering (4.3), we conclude that

ℙ⁡[BF]⩽ 5​Δ−500.\mathbb{P}[B_{F}]\,\leqslant\,5\Delta^{-500}.

Since this bound holds for all F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}, it follows that 𝗉⁡(ℬ)⩽5​Δ−500\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant 5\Delta^{-500}.

Putting everything together, we see that

𝗉⁡(ℬ)​(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)8⩽ 5​Δ−500⋅2216​Δ40= 5⋅2216⋅Δ−460⩽ 5⋅2−244< 2−15,\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\,(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)^{8}\,\leqslant\,5\Delta^{-500}\cdot 2^{216}\Delta^{40}\,=\,5\cdot 2^{216}\cdot\Delta^{-460}\,\leqslant\,5\cdot 2^{-244}\,<\,2^{-15},

4.4.  Edge-colorings of Schreier graphs

In this subsection, we derive Theorem 1.51 from Theorem 1.53. The main idea of the proof of Theorem 1.51 is to decompose the line graph L⁡(G)L(G) of GG into certain induced subgraphs with a simple structure and then combine colorings of those subgraphs into a coloring of L⁡(G)L(G). We begin with a couple lemmas that facilitate this approach. The following observation is almost trivial:

Lemma 4.3.

Let GG be a Borel graph and let V⁡(G)=U1⊔…⊔UnV(G)=U_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup U_{n} be a partition of the vertex set of GG into Borel subsets such that χ𝖡​(G⁡[Ui])<∞\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G[U_{i}])<\infty for all 1⩽i⩽n1\leqslant i\leqslant n. Then

χ𝖡​(G)⩽∑i=1nχ𝖡​(G⁡[Ui]).\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\,\leqslant\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G[U_{i}]).
Proof.

Let qi≔χ𝖡​(G⁡[Ui])q_{i}\coloneqq\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G[U_{i}]) and let fi:Ui→qif_{i}\colon U_{i}\to q_{i} be a Borel proper qiq_{i}-coloring of G⁡[Ui]G[U_{i}]. Define

fi′​(v)≔fi​(v)+∑j=1i−1qjfor all ​v∈Ui.f_{i}^{\prime}(v)\,\coloneqq\,f_{i}(v)+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}q_{j}\quad\text{for all }v\in U_{i}.

Then f≔f1′⊔…⊔fn′f\coloneqq f_{1}^{\prime}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup f_{n}^{\prime} is a Borel proper (∑i=1nqi)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}q_{i}\right)-coloring of GG. ∎

For a graph GG, let Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) denote the maximum degree of GG. If in the setting of Lemma 4.3 each graph G⁡[Ui]G[U_{i}] has finite maximum degree, then we can use Theorem 1.5 to write

χ𝖡​(G)⩽∑i=1nχ𝖡​(G⁡[Ui])⩽∑i=1n(Δ⁡(G⁡[Ui])+1)=n+∑i=1nΔ⁡(G⁡[Ui]).\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\,\leqslant\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G[U_{i}])\,\leqslant\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\Delta(G[U_{i}])+1)\,=\,n+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Delta(G[U_{i}]).

The next lemma, which we deduce from Theorem 1.53, allows us to improve this bound when GG has finite asymptotic separation index and the graphs G⁡[Ui]G[U_{i}] do not have small components:

Lemma 4.4.

Let GG be a Borel graph of maximum degree at most Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}, where Δ⩾2\Delta\geqslant 2, and let V⁡(G)=U1⊔…⊔UnV(G)=U_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup U_{n} be a partition of the vertex set of GG into Borel subsets. Suppose that for all 1⩽i⩽n1\leqslant i\leqslant n, every component of G⁡[Ui]G[U_{i}] contains at least 225​Δ​log⁡Δ2^{25}\,\Delta\log\Delta vertices. If 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty, then

χ𝖡​(G)⩽ 1+∑i=1nΔ⁡(G⁡[Ui]).\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\,\leqslant\,1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Delta(G[U_{i}]).
Proof.

Let G′G^{\prime} be the spanning subgraph of GG with E⁡(G′)≔E⁡(G⁡[U1])⊔…⊔E⁡(G⁡[Un])E(G^{\prime})\coloneqq E(G[U_{1}])\sqcup\ldots\sqcup E(G[U_{n}]). Applying Theorem 1.53 with H=G1=GH=G_{1}=G and G2=G′G_{2}=G^{\prime} yields a Borel GG-independent complete section SS for G′G^{\prime}. For each 1⩽i⩽n1\leqslant i\leqslant n, let Ui′≔Ui∖SU_{i}^{\prime}\coloneqq U_{i}\setminus S. Clearly, Δ⁡(G⁡[Ui′])⩽Δ⁡(G⁡[Ui])\Delta(G[U_{i}^{\prime}])\leqslant\Delta(G[U_{i}]). Moreover, since SS meets every connected component of G⁡[Ui]G[U_{i}], every component of G⁡[Ui′]G[U_{i}^{\prime}] includes a vertex that is adjacent to SS in G⁡[Ui]G[U_{i}] and hence has degree at most Δ⁡(G⁡[Ui])−1\Delta(G[U_{i}])-1 in G⁡[Ui′]G[U_{i}^{\prime}]. Therefore, by a result of Conley, Marks, and Tucker-Drob [CMT16, p. 16, proof of Theorem 1.2], χ𝖡​(G⁡[Ui′])⩽Δ⁡(G⁡[Ui])\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G[U_{i}^{\prime}])\leqslant\Delta(G[U_{i}]).

To finish the argument, we apply Lemma 4.3 to the partition V⁡(G)=S⊔U1′⊔…⊔Un′V(G)=S\sqcup U_{1}^{\prime}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup U_{n}^{\prime} to get

χ𝖡​(G)⩽χ𝖡​(G⁡[S])+∑i=1nχ𝖡​(G⁡[Ui′])⩽ 1+∑i=1nΔ⁡(G⁡[Ui]).∎\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\,\leqslant\,\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G[S])+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G[U_{i}^{\prime}])\,\leqslant\,1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Delta(G[U_{i}]).\qed

For the remainder of §4.4, we fix a group Γ\Gamma generated by a finite symmetric set F⊆Γ∖{𝟏Γ}F\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\{\mathbf{1}_{\Gamma}\}. For ease of reference, let us restate Theorem 1.51 here:

Theorem 1.51.

Suppose that |F|⩾2|F|\geqslant 2 and for each σ∈F\sigma\in F, the order of σ\sigma is either even or at least 230​|F|​log⁡|F|2^{30}\,|F|\log|F|. Let 𝒂:Γ⮌X\bm{a}\colon\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free Borel action of Γ\Gamma on a standard Borel space XX and let G≔𝖲𝖼𝗁⁡(𝒂,F)G\coloneqq\mathsf{Sch}(\bm{a},F) be the corresponding Schreier graph. If 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty, then χ𝖡′​(G)⩽|F|+1\chi^{\prime}_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\leqslant|F|+1.

Proof.

Recall that the line graph of GG is the graph L⁡(G)L(G) with vertex set E⁡(G)E(G) and edge set {{e,e′}∈[E⁡(G)]2:|e∩e′|=1}\{\{e,e^{\prime}\}\in[E(G)]^{2}\,:\,|e\cap e^{\prime}|=1\}. Note that we have χ𝖡′​(G)=χ𝖡​(L⁡(G))\chi^{\prime}_{\mathsf{B}}(G)=\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(L(G)). To bound χ𝖡​(L​(G))\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(L(G)), we shall apply Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4 to certain partitions of E⁡(G)E(G).

To begin with, we show that 𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(L⁡(G))⩽𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞\mathsf{asi}(L(G))\leqslant\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty. Set s≔𝖺𝗌𝗂⁡(G)<∞s\coloneqq\mathsf{asi}(G)<\infty. By the Luzin–Novikov theorem (Theorem 2.2), there is a Borel function c:E⁡(G)→Xc\colon E(G)\to X such that c⁡(e)∈ec(e)\in e for all e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G). Take any R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}} and let X=U0⊔…⊔UsX=U_{0}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup U_{s} be a partition witnessing that 𝗌𝗂⁡(GR+1)⩽s\mathsf{si}(G^{R+1})\leqslant s. Define a partition E⁡(G)=E0⊔…⊔EsE(G)=E_{0}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup E_{s} by Ei≔c−1​(Ui)E_{i}\coloneqq c^{-1}(U_{i}). If ee, e′∈E⁡(G)e^{\prime}\in E(G) are joined by a path of length at most RR in L⁡(G)L(G), then c⁡(e)c(e) and c⁡(e′)c(e^{\prime}) are joined by a path of length at most R+1R+1 in GG. It follows that the graphs L​(G)R​[Ei]L(G)^{R}[E_{i}] are component-finite, and hence 𝗌𝗂⁡(L​(G)R)⩽s\mathsf{si}(L(G)^{R})\leqslant s, as desired.

Let F2F_{2} be the set of all generators σ∈F\sigma\in F of order 22 and let F>2⊆F∖F2F_{>2}\subseteq F\setminus F_{2} be a subset formed by picking one member from each pair {σ,σ−1}⊆F∖F2\{\sigma,\sigma^{-1}\}\subseteq F\setminus F_{2}. Then we have

|F|=|F2|+2​|F>2|.|F|\,=\,|F_{2}|+2|F_{>2}|.

We split the set F>2F_{>2} as F>2=F𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗇⊔F𝗈𝖽𝖽⊔F∞F_{>2}=F_{\mathsf{even}}\sqcup F_{\mathsf{odd}}\sqcup F_{\infty}, where F𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗇F_{\mathsf{even}}, F𝗈𝖽𝖽F_{\mathsf{odd}}, and F∞F_{\infty} comprise the elements σ∈F>2\sigma\in F_{>2} whose order is even, odd, or infinite respectively. For σ∈F2∪F>2\sigma\in F_{2}\cup F_{>2}, define

Eσ≔{{x,σ⋅𝒂x}:x∈X}.E_{\sigma}\,\coloneqq\,\{\{x,\sigma\cdot_{\bm{a}}x\}\,:\,x\in X\}.

Note that the sets (Eσ:σ∈F2∪F>2)(E_{\sigma}\,:\,\sigma\in F_{2}\cup F_{>2}) form a partition of E⁡(G)E(G).

Let Lσ≔L⁡(G)​[Eσ]L_{\sigma}\coloneqq L(G)[E_{\sigma}]. If σ∈F2\sigma\in F_{2}, then EσE_{\sigma} is an L⁡(G)L(G)-independent set. For σ∈F𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗇∪F𝗈𝖽𝖽\sigma\in F_{\mathsf{even}}\cup F_{\mathsf{odd}}, every component of LσL_{\sigma} is a cycle of length ord⁡(σ)\mathrm{ord}(\sigma), and for σ∈F∞\sigma\in F_{\infty}, every component of LσL_{\sigma} is an infinite path. If σ∉F∞\sigma\not\in F_{\infty}, then LσL_{\sigma} is component-finite and hence, by Corollary 2.3, χ𝖡​(Lσ)=χ⁡(Lσ)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(L_{\sigma})=\chi(L_{\sigma}).

Let L0L_{0} and L1L_{1} be the subgraphs of L⁡(G)L(G) induced by ⋃σ∈F2∪F𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗇Eσ\bigcup_{\sigma\in F_{2}\cup F_{\mathsf{even}}}E_{\sigma} and ⋃σ∈F𝗈𝖽𝖽∪F∞Eσ\bigcup_{\sigma\in F_{\mathsf{odd}}\cup F_{\infty}}E_{\sigma} respectively. By Lemma 4.3,

χ𝖡​(L0)⩽∑σ∈F2∪F𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗇χ𝖡​(Lσ)=|F2|+2​|F𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗇|.\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(L_{0})\,\leqslant\,\sum_{\sigma\in F_{2}\cup F_{\mathsf{even}}}\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(L_{\sigma})\,=\,|F_{2}|+2|F_{\mathsf{even}}|.

Note that Δ⁡(L⁡(G))<2​|F|\Delta(L(G))<2|F|. Since every component of LσL_{\sigma} for σ∈F𝗈𝖽𝖽∪F∞\sigma\in F_{\mathsf{odd}}\cup F_{\infty} contains at least

230​|F|​log|F|⩾ 225⋅2​|F|​log⁡(2​|F|)2^{30}\,|F|\log|F|\,\geqslant\,2^{25}\cdot 2|F|\log(2|F|)

vertices, we may apply Lemma 4.4 to conclude that

χ𝖡​(L1)⩽ 1+∑σ∈F𝗈𝖽𝖽∪F∞Δ⁡(Lσ)= 1+2​|F𝗈𝖽𝖽|+2​|F∞|.\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(L_{1})\,\leqslant\,1+\sum_{\sigma\in F_{\mathsf{odd}}\cup F_{\infty}}\Delta(L_{\sigma})\,=\,1+2|F_{\mathsf{odd}}|+2|F_{\mathsf{\infty}}|.

By Lemma 4.3 again,

χ𝖡​(L⁡(G))⩽χ𝖡​(L0)+χ𝖡​(L1)⩽|F2​|+2​|F𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗇|+1+2|​F𝗈𝖽𝖽​|+2|​F∞|=|F|+1,\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(L(G))\,\leqslant\,\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(L_{0})\,+\,\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(L_{1})\,\leqslant\,|F_{2}|+2|F_{\mathsf{even}}|+1+2|F_{\mathsf{odd}}|+2|F_{\mathsf{\infty}}|\,=\,|F|+1,

and the proof is complete. ∎
